_readme: Plain-language overlay for the "simpler wording" accessibility option (~5th-grade reading level). Mirrors the normal catalog key-for-key, but ONLY where a simpler wording exists — anything absent falls back to the normal text, so partial coverage is safe. Data content (animal diets, habitats, ecology) goes under "content", exactly like the translation overlay.

coreLoop.text: Here is the loop. Gather stuff. Craft it into homes for animals. Place it. Then animals come back on their own. First, a grasshopper.
coreLoop.touch: Here is the loop. Gather stuff. Craft it into homes for animals. Place it. Then animals come back on their own. First, a grasshopper.

basket.text: Press B to see what you are carrying. Your basket only holds so much. When it is full, put extra in a chest. The bar at the bottom switches tools. You can also press 1, 2, or 3.
basket.touch: Tap the basket button to see what you are carrying. Your basket only holds so much. When it is full, put extra in a chest. The bar at the bottom switches tools.

chest.text: Walk to the chest by your tent. Press E or Space to open it. Put spare stuff in when your basket is full. You can still craft with it from anywhere, so you do not need to carry it.
chest.touch: Walk to the chest by your tent and tap it. Put spare stuff in when your basket is full. You can still craft with it from anywhere, so you do not need to carry it.

crafting.touch: Tap the hammer button to open crafting. It uses your basket from anywhere. Now let us build the grasshopper a home.

toolbelt.text: Your tools are at the bottom. 1 is the basket to gather. 2 is the shovel to dig. 3 is the watering can. Press T to open Tools. Spend materials there to make them better. Better ones gather and dig more. This area's guide is on the same page.
toolbelt.touch: Your tools are at the bottom. The basket gathers. The shovel digs. The watering can waters. Tap the tools button to make each one better. Better tools gather more and dig more. Some upgrades open up as land gets healthier.

tools.text: Press T to open Tools. Spend stuff to make your basket, shovel, watering can, or journal better. Better tools gather more and dig more. They also unlock the next field journal tier. Some upgrades open up as land gets healthier.
tools.touch: Tap the tools button to open Tools. Spend stuff to make your basket, shovel, watering can, or journal better. Better tools gather more and dig more. Some upgrades open up as land gets healthier.

journal.text: Press J to open your journal. It shows every animal that can come back to each area. It also shows who came back. Each area has one guide. Write it up once to open the whole page for each animal. Write it up again to see exactly what each animal is waiting for. You do that in Tools.
journal.touch: Tap the journal button. It shows every animal that can come back to each area and who came back. Each area has one guide. Write it up once to open the whole page. Write it up again to see what each animal is waiting for. You do that in Tools.

map.text: Press M to open the Preserve. It tracks how healthy each area is and who lives there. It shows what you need to open the next one. You can also travel back to any area you have been. Tap the walk icon on its row.
map.touch: Tap the map button to open the Preserve. It tracks how healthy each area is and who lives there. It shows what you need to open the next one. You can also travel back to any area you have been.

menus.text: Your menus are at the top right. Learn holds your journal and stars. Build holds your basket, crafting, tools, and goals. World holds the map and weather. Each one explains itself the first time you open it.
menus.touch: Your menus are at the top right. Learn holds your journal and stars. Build holds your basket, crafting, tools, and goals. World holds the map and weather. Each one explains itself the first time you open it.

proximity.text: Here is a secret. Animals come back to neighborhoods, not to single pieces. Put food, water, and shelter close together. A patch by a pond by a shrub works well. Far more animals will move in that way.
proximity.touch: Here is a secret. Animals come back to neighborhoods, not to single pieces. Put food, water, and shelter close together. A patch by a pond by a shrub works well. Far more animals will move in that way.

star.text: That is the whole loop. The grasshopper just earned your first star, First Friend. There are 50 stars to find. You earn them for healing land, bringing back big animals, and mastering tools. They are not easy. Press K to see them all. New ones go to the top. Next, a quick look at your other menus.
star.touch: That is the whole loop. The grasshopper just earned your first star, First Friend. There are 50 stars to find. You earn them for healing land, bringing back big animals, and mastering tools. They are not easy. Tap the star button to see them all. Next, a quick look at your other menus.

home.text: One last thing. Walk back to your tent and press E to go inside. The sign by the tent turns your tent into a real house. Each style gives its own bonus. After that you can upgrade four things: Space lets you carry more, Comfort makes your bonus stronger, plus Decor and Light. More upgrades open as your land gets healthier. Inside you can place things you craft. Go in now. The preserve is yours. Have fun!

weather.text: Press N to open the Weather guide. Each area has its own weather. It changes on its own and drifts with the seasons. The guide shows what is happening everywhere. It also explains how weather and season shape the area you are in. Watch the sky. Odd weather can leave rare stuff to gather while it lasts.
weather.touch: Tap the cloud button to open the Weather guide. Each area has its own weather. It changes on its own and drifts with the seasons. Watch the sky. Odd weather can leave rare stuff to gather while it lasts.

settings.simpleTextHint: Uses short sentences and everyday words all through the game. That includes the animal notes. Nothing is hidden. It is just said in a simpler way.
settings.reduceMotionHint: Stops menu animations, rain and snow, camera moves, and the day and night light change. The view stays still and evenly lit.

colorblindHint.off: Pick the type that fits you. The game changes its colors, raises contrast, and labels the weather and time of day. Then nothing depends on color alone.
colorblindHint.redgreen: Red and green is the most common type. Reds and greens look alike. This moves those colors apart, raises contrast, adds text labels, and holds the light steady.
colorblindHint.blueyellow: Blue and yellow is more rare. Blues and greens look alike, and so do yellows and pinks. This moves those colors apart, raises contrast, adds text labels, and holds the light steady.
colorblindHint.mono: This type means seeing little or no color. The game turns black and white. It uses contrast, outlines, and text labels instead of color.

nextbiome.hint: Check off each thing below to open {biome}.

red-fox.hint: This one comes back once smaller animals are here. It needs cover for a den and a healthy meadow.
red-fox.diet: Voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and bugs. Also berries
red-fox.preferredHabitat: Meadows, farm edges, and hedges across open land
red-fox.fact: When hunting mice, red foxes tend to pounce facing northeast. They seem to use the Earth like a compass to judge the jump.
red-fox.role: A clever mid-sized hunter that keeps mice and rabbits in check. It stalks low, then pounces. It also eats bugs, berries, and dead animals. No bigger hunters live here, so the fox sits near the top.

ladybug.hint: Plant a patch of clover. The aphids show up on their own, and that is the whole invitation.
ladybug.diet: aphids and other small, soft bugs
ladybug.shelter: Winters in leaf litter in big groups. Rests on leaves
ladybug.fact: One ladybug can eat about 5,000 aphids in its life. That is about 50 a day.
ladybug.role: A small hunter that eats aphids and other soft bugs, both when young and when grown. That makes it a great helper in gardens. Birds and bigger bugs then eat it, which links the aphids up the food web.

western-meadowlark.hint: Wide, unbroken native grass and a tall perch to sing from. Leave out the shrubs — woody cover is what pushes this one away.
western-meadowlark.diet: Mostly bugs in summer. Seeds and grain in winter
western-meadowlark.role: A grassland bird that eats lots of grasshoppers, crickets, and beetles in summer. In winter it eats seeds. All that eating keeps bug numbers down. It is round and feeds on the ground, so hawks and other meadow hunters catch it.

red-tailed-hawk.hint: A tall tree to nest in. Open grass to hunt over. And plenty of small animals already there.
red-tailed-hawk.diet: voles, ground squirrels and rabbits. Also birds and snakes
red-tailed-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open land: grassland, fields, and meadows seen from above
red-tailed-hawk.fact: That sharp eagle cry in movies is almost always a red-tailed hawk.
red-tailed-hawk.role: The top day hunter of the meadow. It rides the wind on wide wings or watches from a perch. By eating voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, and birds it keeps plant eaters in check. Almost nothing hunts a grown hawk here.

barn-owl.hint: A quiet, healthy meadow with lots of voles and a dark place to rest.
barn-owl.diet: Almost all small mammals: voles, mice, and shrews, hunted at night
barn-owl.shelter: Nests in tree holes, cliff cracks, and quiet buildings
barn-owl.fact: A barn owl’s heart-shaped face guides sound so well it can catch prey in the dark by ear alone.
barn-owl.role: The night hunter of mice. It flies low and silent over the grass and swallows mice whole, which keeps mouse numbers down. Nothing here hunts it.

woodpecker.hint: Small dead stubs with the wood already gone soft. It cannot chisel healthy timber, so leave the rotting stuff standing.
woodpecker.diet: Mostly bugs: beetle grubs, ants, and caterpillars. Some berries and sap
woodpecker.shelter: Holes it cuts itself in dead standing trees. Sleeps in them all year
woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Open leafy and mixed woods with dead trees full of bugs
woodpecker.fact: The downy woodpecker is small. It can dig into weed galls for fly grubs. Bigger woodpeckers cannot reach them.
woodpecker.role: Woodpeckers eat the beetles and bugs that live in wood and bark, which takes pressure off the trees. The holes they leave behind become homes for nuthatches, wrens, and flying squirrels. Hawks, owls, squirrels, and snakes hunt them.

great-horned-owl.hint: Tall trees, quiet shelter, and prey animals that are already back.
great-horned-owl.diet: Mammals and birds: rabbits, voles, squirrels, skunks. Also frogs
great-horned-owl.preferredHabitat: Old woods broken up by open ground, in almost every area
great-horned-owl.fact: Great horned owls are one of the few hunters that kill and eat skunks. The spray does not seem to bother them.
great-horned-owl.role: This owl sits at the top of the forest at night. It eats a wider range of prey than any other owl or hawk in North America. It holds down rabbits, squirrels, chipmunks, and even other owls, so those numbers jump when it is gone. Nothing hunts the adults, only the eggs and chicks.

black-bear.hint: A full pantry and a winter bed: heavy berry crops, oaks that drop acorns, water, and a den under the roots of a fallen tree.
black-bear.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, roots, rock cracks, or dug holes. Sleeps all winter
black-bear.preferredHabitat: Thick forest with dense brush and lots of berries and nuts
black-bear.fact: Black bear cubs are born in winter sleep and weigh under half a pound. That is the smallest newborn compared to adult size of any furry animal.
black-bear.role: Black bears eat almost anything. They spread berry seeds, dig up bugs, and now and then take deer and elk babies. They are the most common big meat eater in North American forests. They tie the nut, bug, and animal layers together. Nothing hunts a grown bear.

elk.hint: Grassy clearings and water in a healthy forest.
elk.shelter: No den. Calves hide in thick plants. The herd watches out together
elk.preferredHabitat: Grassy clearings and open wood edges inside a bigger forest
elk.fact: In Yellowstone, elk are about 85% of what wolves eat in winter. Their leftovers feed at least a dozen other animals.
elk.role: Elk are big grazers. Heavy grazing shapes grass, willow, and aspen, and those plants come back when elk numbers drop. They are the main food of wolves, big cats, and bears, so they hold the big hunters up, and when one dies many scavengers eat. Their yearly moves spread goodness up and down the mountain.

bobcat.hint: Thick low brush to sneak through, a sheltered rock den for the kittens, and plenty of prey already back.
bobcat.diet: only meat: rabbits, mice, and squirrels. Some birds and lizards
bobcat.preferredHabitat: Forest with thick brush, scrub, and rocky ground
bobcat.fact: In the eastern US, bobcat numbers rise and fall with how many rabbits there are.
bobcat.role: Bobcats are key mid-sized hunters. They hold down rabbits, mice, and squirrels, which eases the pressure on forest plants. They sit below cougars and wolves and above the small animals they take. They shape whole groups of small animals.

ratsnake.hint: Big rough-barked trees are the whole trick. It hunts up them as much as under them. Leave a heap of rotting wood chips at the foot of a stump for her eggs. No pond needed.
ratsnake.diet: Mice, voles, chipmunks, and young squirrels. Also birds and eggs taken straight from nests
ratsnake.shelter: Hollow trunks, rot pockets, and stump cavities. The eggs go in a warm heap of rotting wood chips
ratsnake.fact: It can climb straight up a bare trunk with nothing to hold onto. It wedges the edges of its belly scales into the ridges in the bark and walks up the side of the tree.
ratsnake.role: The forest's rodent brake, and the only hunter here that works up high and down low. On the ground it eats mice, voles, and chipmunks by the dozen. Up in the trees it raids old woodpecker holes and songbird nests, so every bird nearby mobs it. It has no venom. It wraps and squeezes. If it gets startled it goes stiff and looks exactly like a fallen branch. She never sits on her eggs. She buries them in rotting wood and lets the heat of the rot do the work. Foxes, fishers, and great horned owls eat it.

beaver.hint: Water channels you have fixed, mud banks, and woody plants.
beaver.diet: Bark and soft wood from willow and aspen, plus water plants
beaver.fact: Beaver dams make wetlands that hold water and support hundreds of other kinds of life.
beaver.role: The builder of the wetland. By cutting trees and damming streams, beavers make new ponds, raise the water, and build the home that most marsh animals need.

minnow.hint: Clean pools joined together with reeds bring fish back. Then everyone who eats fish follows.
minnow.fact: Minnow schools are the base that herons, otters, and mink all depend on.
minnow.role: The base of the wetland food web. These small schooling fish eat algae, plankton, and bug babies. Then almost every marsh hunter eats them.

burrowing-owl.hint: It cannot dig. Bring back a digger first. Then it needs low, open ground to hunt.
burrowing-owl.fact: It makes a rasping call like a rattlesnake to scare visitors out of its burrow.
burrowing-owl.role: A small owl that lives in holes other animals dug. It hunts bugs by day and mice by night, so it holds down both. Badgers, coyotes, and snakes hunt it.

white-tailed-ptarmigan.hint: Alpine shrubs and quiet cover to nest in, with frostflowers in bloom.
white-tailed-ptarmigan.preferredHabitat: High open ground above the trees all year. Winters in willow hollows
white-tailed-ptarmigan.fact: It is the only bird in North America that lives above the tree line all year.
white-tailed-ptarmigan.role: A mountain bird that hides so well you can walk right past it. It eats buds, leaves, and seeds, and lives almost only on willow in winter. Each winter it grows feathered snowshoes on its feet. Eagles, foxes, weasels, and martens hunt it and its chicks.

golden-eagle.hint: This one comes last, once the high country is truly alive again. It needs a real cliff to nest on and open ground below with plenty moving on it.
golden-eagle.diet: Marmots, hares, ground squirrels, and birds. Also dead animals
golden-eagle.preferredHabitat: Open high country with cliffs and plenty of mid-sized prey
golden-eagle.fact: Golden eagles sometimes line the nest with leaves that smell sweet. It may keep bugs away.
golden-eagle.role: The top hunter of the high country. It drops from the sky on marmots, hares, white-tailed ptarmigan, and even small meat eaters. It only shows up when the mountain is full of prey. Almost nothing hunts a grown eagle.

sea-otter.hint: Living kelp to wrap up in, calm water to clean its fur in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Dead kelp on the sand is no use.
sea-otter.diet: sea urchins most of all. Also crabs, mussels and sea stars
sea-otter.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with lots of shellfish
sea-otter.role: A key animal of the coast. By eating sea urchins it stops them from mowing down the kelp. So kelp forests and everything living in them can thrive. It also eats a lot of mussels and clams along the rocks.

gray-whale.hint: Deep water and a sea floor thick with tiny shrimp-like animals. Tidepools and dune plants will never bring this one in.
gray-whale.diet: Tiny shrimp-like animals, strained out of the sea floor mud
gray-whale.fact: Gray whales travel up to 14,000 miles there and back. That is one of the longest trips of any mammal.
gray-whale.role: A whale that feeds on the sea floor. It rolls on its side, sucks up mud, and strains out tiny shrimp-like animals. Killer whales are its main danger. A whale passing by means the coast is fully healed.

leopard-frog.hint: A lily pool and a few open water tiles.
leopard-frog.fact: Leopard frogs escape with wild zig-zag leaps straight back into the water.
leopard-frog.role: A wide-mouthed frog. It eats almost any small animal it can swallow, even other frogs. Herons, mink, and snakes need it for food.

boreal-toad.hint: A snowmelt pool and a few open water tiles.
boreal-toad.diet: Beetles, ants, flies, and other small crawlers. Tadpoles eat algae
boreal-toad.preferredHabitat: High wet meadows with open pools to breed in
boreal-toad.fact: Rocky Mountain boreal toads have crashed because of a deadly skin fungus.
boreal-toad.role: The only toad of the high country. It eats bugs, breeds in shallow snowmelt pools, and takes years to grow up. Its tadpoles eat algae. A skin fungus has wiped out many southern groups, so people work hard to save it.

elf-owl.hint: A cactus is not enough. Something has to drill the hole first.
elf-owl.fact: The world’s smallest owl pulls the stinger off scorpions before eating them.
elf-owl.role: The smallest owl in the world. It hunts bugs and scorpions at night and nests in old woodpecker holes. Snakes and bigger owls are a danger to it.

mountain-chickadee.hint: Plant a subalpine fir and a bent pine with mountain flowers.
mountain-chickadee.diet: Bugs and spiders in summer. Pine seeds and nuts in fall and winter
mountain-chickadee.shelter: Old woodpecker holes and tree holes in pines and aspens
mountain-chickadee.role: A busy little bird that picks bugs off pine twigs and lives on seeds it hid away in winter. Mixed flocks often form around it, and it spreads pine seeds. Small hawks, weasels, and martens eat it and its chicks.

rock-squirrel.hint: It is only above ground for half the year, so look in the warm months. Give it seed-heavy flowers to fatten on, rock to duck into, and diggable ground under a boulder for the long sleep.
rock-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Sunny rocky slopes, loose rock edges, and open dwarf pine at and above the tree line
rock-squirrel.fact: People call it a giant chipmunk, but it has no stripes on its cheeks. In winter it cools until it is barely above freezing and its heart beats only a few times a minute.
rock-squirrel.role: A stripe-backed seed eater. It spends the short summer eating until it is round, then vanishes underground for half the year. It buries seeds all over the slope and forgets enough of them to replant it. It also digs up and eats underground fungi, so the spores ride through its gut and get planted somewhere new. Ermines, martens, lynx, and eagles all hunt it.

black-turnstone.hint: Tidepools and kelp wrack with a driftwood pile to hide in.
black-turnstone.fact: Turnstones flip over stones and shells to grab the creatures hiding beneath.
black-turnstone.role: A shore bird that pries barnacles and limpets loose. It also flips seaweed to find food hidden under it. It helps hold down shore bug numbers, and it needs rich rocky shores.

bat-star.hint: A couple of tidepools with an eelgrass bed.
bat-star.role: A sea star that eats almost anything. It pushes its stomach out over the sea floor to break down algae and dead animals. It is the cleanup crew of the shallows. It keeps tidepools and eelgrass beds tidy.

cottontail-rabbit.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with bushes to dash into
cottontail-rabbit.fact: Cottontails rest in shallow dips in the ground called forms. They do not dig burrows.
cottontail-rabbit.role: A grass eater that most meadow hunters depend on. It feeds on grass, clover, and twigs, and it has many babies to make up for how many are eaten. Foxes, hawks, owls, and badgers all live on rabbits.

monarch-butterfly.diet: Young ones eat only milkweed. Adults drink flower nectar
monarch-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed and flowers
monarch-butterfly.fact: Monarchs travel up to 3,000 miles. No one butterfly makes the whole trip. It takes a few lifetimes.
monarch-butterfly.role: This butterfly lays eggs only on milkweed. Milkweed is poisonous. The poison stays in the caterpillar and in the grown butterfly. Bright orange wings warn birds to keep away, so almost nothing eats it. Adults feed on late flowers and move pollen.

song-sparrow.diet: Bugs in summer. Seeds and fruit all year
song-sparrow.fact: A male song sparrow can learn about 20 tunes and sing hundreds of versions of them.
song-sparrow.role: A small ground bird that eats bugs while nesting and seeds and fruit the rest of the year. So it keeps bugs down and spreads seeds. There are lots of them, so meadow hawks and snakes eat them often. They link the tiny life on the ground to the big hunters.

mule-deer.shelter: Sleeps in bushes, tall grass, or forest edges. No den
mule-deer.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrubland with food and water close by
mule-deer.fact: Mule deer are named for their big, mule-like ears. Each ear turns on its own to find where a sound came from.
mule-deer.role: A big plant eater that shapes the meadow by eating shrubs and leaves. Its eating and its droppings feed the soil and keep plants in check. The animals that would hunt it do not live in this meadow, so little bothers it here.

ground-squirrel.diet: Mostly seeds, grass, and flowers, plus bugs like grasshoppers
ground-squirrel.shelter: Big burrows with many doors, dug in open ground
ground-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadows and slopes near rocks to watch from
ground-squirrel.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, these squirrels kick sand and wave hot tails. The heat jams the snake’s way of seeing.
ground-squirrel.role: A digging animal that eats seeds, greens, and bugs. Its holes let air into the soil, and old holes become homes for others. Hawks, foxes, snakes, and badgers all hunt it. Its towns hold the meadow food web together.

garter-snake.diet: Worms, frogs, slugs, small fish, bugs, and small mice
garter-snake.shelter: Hides under rocks and logs. Winters in shared dens
garter-snake.fact: Garter snakes have a mild venom for their tiny prey. They are harmless to people.
garter-snake.role: A common meadow hunter that eats worms, frogs, fish, bugs, and small mice. Its spit is a little poisonous, just enough to slow small prey. It keeps bugs and frogs in check. Hawks, owls, and foxes eat it.

bumblebee.diet: nectar and pollen, from many kinds of flower
bumblebee.shelter: Nests in old mouse burrows, grass clumps, or holes in the ground
bumblebee.fact: Bumblebees shake their flight muscles to knock pollen loose. Tomatoes and blueberries need this to make fruit.
bumblebee.role: A big, fuzzy bee that visits many kinds of flowers for nectar and pollen. It buzzes to shake pollen loose, which most bees cannot do. That makes it key to meadow plants. Spiders and birds hunt it.

grasshopper.diet: plants: grasses, sedges, and broad-leaved weeds
grasshopper.fact: Grasshoppers hear through eardrums on their belly, not their head.
grasshopper.role: The main plant eater of the meadow and the main food too. It turns grass into food for many hunters. Birds, snakes, mammals, and other bugs all eat it. When grasshoppers boom, the whole food web feels it.

tree-squirrel.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, tree buds, and fungi. Sometimes bugs and eggs
tree-squirrel.shelter: Dens in tree holes and leaf nests built high up
tree-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Old leafy or mixed forest full of oaks and hickories
tree-squirrel.fact: Gray squirrels bury thousands of nuts each year. The ones they forget grow into new trees.
tree-squirrel.role: Squirrels eat a lot of seeds. But they also bury nuts and forget them, and those nuts grow into new trees. They spread helpful fungus too, and now and then they raid bird nests. There are so many of them that almost every forest hunter eats them.

forest-salamander.diet: Small crawlers: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants, and worms
forest-salamander.shelter: Under logs, rocks, and damp leaves. Hides in soil holes
forest-salamander.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp forest floor with lots of fallen wood
forest-salamander.fact: In some woods, all these tiny salamanders together weigh more than all the birds.
forest-salamander.role: This little salamander rules the leaf litter. It eats the tiny mites and springtails that break down dead leaves. There are so many of them that snakes, birds, and small mammals count on them for food. It breathes through its skin, so it shows whether the forest is damp and healthy.

gray-fox.diet: Mice, voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and eggs. In late summer, a huge amount of fruit
gray-fox.shelter: Hollow logs, rock cracks, and old dens. It will also curl up on a high branch
gray-fox.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and old clearings growing back, with tangled cover to climb
gray-fox.fact: It is the only dog in the world that climbs trees. It hooks its curved claws into the bark, goes up the trunk like a cat, and naps ten meters up, where nothing that hunts it can follow.
gray-fox.role: The forest's climbing fox. It hunts the brushy edges for mice, rabbits, and ground-nesting birds, then goes straight up a trunk after squirrels, nests, and grapes. By late summer it eats so much fruit that its droppings are half seeds, which plants the next berry tangles all along the edge. Bobcats kill it in the open and great horned owls take its kits, so it always keeps a climbable tree close.

raccoon.diet: what it finds: crayfish, bugs, frogs, fish, small mammals, eggs, and fruit
raccoon.shelter: Likes hollow tree dens. Also rock cracks, burrows, and buildings
raccoon.preferredHabitat: Damp forest near water for finding food
raccoon.fact: A raccoon’s paws have about four times more touch sensors than its eyes have light sensors.
raccoon.role: Raccoons eat almost anything. They hold down crayfish, frogs, and bugs, spread fruit seeds, and raid bird nests. There are lots of them, so they tie the water and the forest together. Coyotes, big owls, and bobcats keep their numbers down.

porcupine.diet: only plants. Inner bark in winter. Buds, twigs, and leaves in summer
porcupine.shelter: Rock dens, hollow logs, and treetops. Uses the same dens each season
porcupine.preferredHabitat: Pine and mixed forest with trees whose bark it can eat
porcupine.fact: The fisher is one of the few hunters that can kill a porcupine. It flips it over to reach the soft belly.
porcupine.role: Porcupines strip bark, which kills or bends trees. That makes dead trees for hole-nesting birds and gives the forest more shapes. They eat nuts, so they share that food with deer and squirrels. Fishers hunt them most, and bobcats and bears eat them now and then.

chipmunk.shelter: Burrows up to 10 m long with rooms for sleeping and food
chipmunk.preferredHabitat: Old leafy forest with logs, stumps, and rocks to hide in
chipmunk.fact: Chipmunks do not really sleep all winter. They wake up to eat from food stores bigger than a bottle of milk.
chipmunk.role: Chipmunks bury seeds in many small spots. So they spread tree seeds and helpful fungus and help the forest grow back. They eat lots of bugs in summer. There are many of them, so everything from weasels to owls eats them. Their holes let air into the soil and shelter other small animals.

nuthatch.diet: Bugs and spiders in summer. Seeds, acorns, and stored nuts in winter
nuthatch.shelter: Tree holes and old woodpecker holes in big trees. Also nest boxes
nuthatch.preferredHabitat: Old leafy and mixed forest with big oaks and hickories
nuthatch.fact: Nuthatches wipe smelly bugs around their nest hole. It may hide their smell from squirrels.
nuthatch.role: Nuthatches eat the bugs that live in bark, like tent caterpillars and wood borers, which helps hold pests down. They wedge acorns and seeds into bark, which moves seeds a short way. They tie the bug layer to the seed layer, and hawks and owls eat them.

banana-slug.diet: Dead leaves, fungus, rot, and droppings. Sometimes young plants
banana-slug.shelter: Under logs and bark. Seals itself in slime when it gets dry
banana-slug.fact: Seeds and fungus spores pass through a banana slug alive. It plants them as it crawls.
banana-slug.role: Banana slugs break down dead leaves and droppings and put the goodness back in the soil. They spread seeds and fungus, so they help both plants and the fungus web that feeds the trees. Their slime numbs mouths, so few animals eat them. Mostly garter snakes and shrews do.

great-blue-heron.diet: Fish, frogs, and small water animals. Also voles and other birds
great-blue-heron.role: The tall, patient watcher of the shallows and the top hunter of the wetland fish. It steps slowly, then strikes faster than you can see.

tiger-salamander.diet: Worms, bugs, small crawlers, and even small animals with backbones
tiger-salamander.fact: The tiger salamander is one of the biggest on land in North America.
tiger-salamander.role: A hungry digger that hunts worms and bugs near its breeding pools. Its young grow in pools with no fish, and they will even eat each other.

dragonfly.diet: Flying bugs as an adult. Young ones in the water eat mosquito young and tadpoles
dragonfly.shelter: Reed stems above water. The young live in the water
dragonfly.role: A top bug hunter both in the air and under water. Adults grab flying bugs. The young live in the water and eat mosquito babies and tiny fish.

water-strider.diet: Bugs caught on the water surface. Also eats dead ones
water-strider.fact: Water striders ride on top of the water. Their legs are covered in thousands of tiny hairs.
water-strider.role: A bug that skates on top of the water. It grabs insects caught in the surface and cleans up dead ones. Fish, frogs, and wading birds catch it easily.

mountain-goat.shelter: Shallow beds scraped into cliff ledges and rocky ground
mountain-goat.preferredHabitat: Steep high cliffs with escape routes above the grass
mountain-goat.role: A sure-footed climber that grazes the highest cliffs. It eats grass, small plants, and lichen off the rock. Its rubbery hooves grip ground that few hunters can follow. Cougars still take young and grown goats, and eagles snatch newborns off ledges.

bighorn-sheep.preferredHabitat: Open grassy mountain slopes next to rough, rocky cliffs
bighorn-sheep.fact: Bighorns escape across rock ledges only a few inches wide.
bighorn-sheep.role: A grazer of open, steep slopes. It crops grass and small plants and stays close to cliffs it can escape into. Rams crash their horns together each fall with a boom you can hear far off. Cougars hunt lambs and adults, and eagles may take the very young.

pika.diet: Grass, weeds, and wildflowers, gathered and dried into hay piles for winter
pika.preferredHabitat: Rock slopes and stone piles next to high flower meadows
pika.fact: Pikas cut and dry little haystacks of plants to eat under the winter snow.
pika.role: A tiny cousin of rabbits that lives in rock piles. It drives the whole mountain food web. All summer it cuts and dries little haystacks of plants so it can eat under the snow. Weasels, martens, foxes, and eagles all hunt it.

yellow-bellied-marmot.preferredHabitat: Open meadow patches with boulders and ground to burrow in
yellow-bellied-marmot.fact: About 98 out of every 100 marmots that die in summer are caught by a hunter.
yellow-bellied-marmot.role: A round rodent that loves to sun itself. It grazes meadow plants and fattens on seeds before sleeping eight months. Groups whistle from boulder lookouts to warn each other. Golden eagles, coyotes, and foxes hunt them.

snowshoe-hare.diet: Green plants in summer. Buds, twigs, bark, and pine needles in winter
snowshoe-hare.shelter: Shallow hollows under thick shrubs and pine cover
snowshoe-hare.preferredHabitat: Brushy thickets and thick undergrowth near open grass
snowshoe-hare.role: A hare of brushy cover near treeline. Its coat flips from brown to white with the seasons. Its numbers rise and fall about every ten years, and hunter numbers rise and fall with them. Martens, foxes, eagles, and owls all hunt it.

grizzly-bear.preferredHabitat: Open high country with soft ground to dig, berry slopes, and no people
grizzly-bear.fact: In late summer grizzly bears climb above the trees to eat moths. They flip rocks to find them, and one bear can eat up to 40,000 in a day.
grizzly-bear.role: It is the biggest animal on the mountain, and that is why everything else stays alert. It digs whole slopes apart looking for roots and ground squirrels, which turns the soil over. In late summer it climbs above the trees to eat moths off the rockslides. It will push a wolverine off a carcass without slowing down.

lynx.shelter: A hollow under rocks, roots, or fallen wood, often started by another animal
lynx.preferredHabitat: High snowy country with thickets of small conifers where hares can hide
lynx.fact: A lynx weighs about as much as a border collie, but its paws are as wide as a mountain lion's. They spread out as it steps, so it walks on top of snow a fox would sink through.
lynx.role: The mountain's hare specialist, and almost nothing else will do. When there are lots of hares, there are lots of lynx. When the hares crash a few years later, the lynx crash right behind them, and the whole cycle repeats about every ten years. It hunts by sitting still in the thickets and waiting for a hare to come close, so low tangled cover matters more to it than open ground. It almost never digs. It moves into a hollow under rock that something else opened. Eagles take its kittens.

pine-marten.diet: Voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, bugs, and berries
pine-marten.fact: Pine martens hunt under the winter snow, in tunnels others cannot reach.
pine-marten.role: A quick weasel of the treeline. It hunts voles, squirrels, pikas, and young hares. It adds berries and bugs in season. It roams over rough forest and rock, and even under the snow. Great horned owls, eagles, and bigger meat eaters hunt it.

nutcracker.preferredHabitat: High pine forest and treeline near pine seeds
nutcracker.fact: It can find thousands of buried seed stores months later, even under snow.
nutcracker.role: A mountain bird that gathers and buries thousands of pine seeds, so it plants the very forest it needs. Its buried food lets it raise chicks in deep winter. It also takes bugs and small animals when it can.

alpine-butterfly.diet: Young ones eat stonecrop. Adults drink from stonecrop and daisies
alpine-butterfly.shelter: No nest. Young hide in leaves and rocks. Eggs wait out the winter
alpine-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Rocky open high slopes where stonecrop grows
alpine-butterfly.fact: Its pale red and black wings warn hunters that it tastes bad.
alpine-butterfly.role: A tough mountain butterfly. Its caterpillars eat only stonecrop, and the adults drink from meadow flowers. Its bright wings warn that it tastes bad. Birds and spiders that ignore the warning still catch a few.

alpine-moth.shelter: Packed by the thousand into cracks under loose rock slabs, out of the sun and the wind
alpine-moth.preferredHabitat: High rockslides beside flower meadows. Summer only; the rest of the year it lives far below
alpine-moth.fact: Every summer millions of these moths fly up out of the lowlands and hide in the rock on the highest peaks. They are so fatty that a bear will spend all day flipping stones to eat them, and can eat forty thousand in a day.
alpine-moth.role: The mountain's fuel delivery. The moths fatten on lowland flowers, then fly hundreds of kilometers uphill to spend the summer in cold rock. Each one arrives as a little parcel of fat, richer than anything that grows up here. Bears, birds, and almost everything that hunts a rockslide eats them. At night they come out to drink nectar and pollinate the high flowers. By dawn they are back under the slabs.

shore-crab.diet: Mostly algae, plus bits of waste, worms, snails, and dead animals
shore-crab.fact: Striped shore crabs eat algae. They also eat dead things, and even each other after they shed their shell.
shore-crab.role: A common shore crab. It scrapes algae off the rocks and cleans up dead animals. Gulls, shorebirds, and bigger crabs all eat it, so it moves food from the algae up to the hunters.

sea-turtle.diet: Mostly sea grass and algae as an adult. Eats more kinds when young
sea-turtle.preferredHabitat: Clean shallow water with sea grass and a quiet beach
sea-turtle.fact: Green sea turtles come back to nest on the same beach where they hatched decades before.
sea-turtle.role: The only sea turtle that eats mostly plants. Adults graze sea grass and algae, which keeps the beds healthy, and the young start out eating both plants and animals. When its eggs do well, the water is clean and the beaches are quiet.

american-goldfinch.diet: Almost all seeds: thistle, sunflower, aster, and grass
american-goldfinch.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open land with thistle, sunflower, and asters
american-goldfinch.fact: Goldfinches eat only plants. They nest late in summer so thistle fluff is ready to line the nest.
american-goldfinch.role: A seed eater that lives on thistle and other flower seeds. So it spreads those seeds across the meadow. It is small and common, so quick hawks and small owls catch it.

bluebird.diet: Mostly bugs off the ground: caterpillars, beetles, crickets. Fruit in winter
bluebird.shelter: A grass-lined nest in tree holes, old woodpecker holes, or boxes
bluebird.fact: An eastern bluebird can spot a tiny bug in the grass 60 feet away. Then it drops down and grabs it.
bluebird.role: A bug eater that nests in tree holes. It watches from a perch, then drops on caterpillars, beetles, and grasshoppers, and eats berries in winter. So it holds bugs down and spreads fruit seeds. It fights for nest holes, and hawks and small owls hunt it.

american-badger.diet: Digs out squirrels, gophers, voles, and mice. Also eats bugs
american-badger.shelter: Digs its own big burrows. A very strong digger
american-badger.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and grassland with soft soil and mice to hunt
american-badger.fact: Badgers sometimes team up with coyotes. The badger digs prey out below while the mountain lion catches the ones that run.
american-badger.role: A meat eater that digs prey right out of their tunnels. That keeps ground squirrel and vole numbers down. The holes it leaves behind help other animals. Almost nothing hunts a grown badger in this meadow.

pileated-woodpecker.diet: Carpenter ants and wood beetle grubs. Also termites, berries, and nuts
pileated-woodpecker.shelter: Cuts a new square nest hole each year in big dead trees
pileated-woodpecker.fact: Its deep square holes can be big enough to snap a small tree in half.
pileated-woodpecker.role: This big woodpecker builds homes for the whole forest. Its large holes become nests for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats, and barred owls. It holds down carpenter ants and beetles. It opens up rotting wood so fungus and other tiny life can get in. Hawks and weasels eat it.

flying-squirrel.diet: Mostly fungus from underground. Also lichen, seeds, nuts, and bugs
flying-squirrel.shelter: Tree holes, old woodpecker holes, and branch nests. Huddles in winter
flying-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Old pine forest with a closed roof of leaves and lots of fungi
flying-squirrel.fact: Fungus spores show up in almost every flying squirrel dropping. It is the forest’s key spreader of them.
flying-squirrel.role: The northern flying squirrel spreads the underground fungus that pine and fir trees need to feed. That teamwork of squirrel, fungus, and tree is what lets the forest grow back. Owls, martens, and fishers eat the squirrel. So food moves from the fungus all the way up to the top hunters.

wood-duck.diet: Acorns, seeds, and water plants. Ducklings also eat bugs and snails
wood-duck.shelter: Only nests in tree holes and nest boxes near water
wood-duck.preferredHabitat: Low leafy woods and wooded swamps with slow water and hollow trees
wood-duck.fact: A day after hatching, wood duck ducklings jump from nest holes up to 50 feet high and land unhurt.
wood-duck.role: Wood ducks tie the flooded woods and the marsh together. They spread acorn and water-plant seeds and hold down the small life of the shallows. Great horned owls, mink, raccoons, and snapping turtles eat them. They nest in old woodpecker holes, so lots of wood ducks means the wooded wetland is healthy.

kingfisher.diet: Small fish and crayfish, plus other water life
kingfisher.fact: Kingfishers dive headfirst into the water with their eyes shut to grab fish.

snapping-turtle.diet: Fish, water plants, dead animals, and almost anything it can catch
snapping-turtle.fact: Almost nothing hunts a grown snapping turtle. They can live for many years.
snapping-turtle.role: A heavy turtle with a hard shell. It waits on the pond bottom and eats almost anything. Grown ones sit near the top of the marsh food web. They eat fish, ducklings, plants, and dead animals.

gray-crowned-rosy-finch.diet: Tiny mountain plant seeds and bugs, often picked off the snow
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.preferredHabitat: High ground above the trees: rock, scree, cliffs, and ice
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.fact: It nests higher than almost any other song bird in North America.
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.role: A high-mountain bird that hops over snow and rock, gathering seeds blown in by the wind and bugs chilled by the cold. It nests in cracks in the rock above treeline. Falcons and hawks are its main danger.

pipit.preferredHabitat: Open high meadows and bare ground during nesting season
pipit.fact: It feeds at the edge of snowbanks, picking up bugs chilled after drifting up from below.
pipit.role: A slim bird that walks across open mountain meadows, bobbing its tail as it hunts bugs. It picks up cold, slow bugs at the edge of snowbanks. Hawks and nest raiders are its main threats.

ermine.diet: Small mice, mostly voles. Also pikas, birds, eggs, and bugs
ermine.role: A small, fierce weasel that lives on voles and other mice, and also takes young pikas and ground-bird eggs. It is thin enough to slip right into their burrows. Foxes, martens, and hawks hunt it in turn.

white-throated-swift.shelter: A cup of feathers glued with its own spit into a narrow crack in a cliff
white-throated-swift.fact: It does everything in the air. It eats, drinks, and even mates in mid-air. A pair locks together and tumbles down the cliff face before letting go.
white-throated-swift.role: A blade-shaped bird that lives in the sky above the mountain. It scoops up moths, beetles, and whatever else the wind lifts, and it is one of the fastest birds in the world in level flight. Its feet cling but never perch, so at night it folds itself into a crack in the cliff. It glues the nest in place with its own spit. It only eats what flies, so a swift working the ridge means the insects below have come back.

fisher.diet: Small and mid-sized mammals: porcupines, hares, squirrels. Also birds and fruit
fisher.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, logs, stumps, and ground burrows. Young go high up
fisher.preferredHabitat: Thick pine and mixed forest with a closed leaf roof and hollow trees
fisher.fact: The fisher is one of the few hunters that kills porcupines. It goes for the face until it can flip it over.
fisher.role: The fisher is a strong mid-level forest hunter. It is one of the few animals that can take a porcupine, which would otherwise damage lots of trees. It fills part of the gap left by big hunters that are gone. When fishers are around, the forest is old and well linked. Bobcats, foxes, and lynx eat the young ones.

praying-mantis.diet: Waits and grabs live bugs, like bees and grasshoppers
praying-mantis.preferredHabitat: Meadows and brushy edges with thick plants to hide in
praying-mantis.fact: A praying mantis can turn its head almost all the way around. No other insect can.
praying-mantis.role: A hunter that sits still and waits, then grabs prey with its spiky front legs faster than you can blink. It eats grasshoppers, bees, beetles, and other bugs, which helps keep bug numbers in check. Birds, garter snakes, and small owls eat it.

skunk.diet: Beetle grubs and bugs dug out of the soil, plus eggs, berries, and mice
skunk.shelter: A borrowed burrow or a hollow under a log. In the coldest weeks it plugs the door with leaves
skunk.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and clearings with soft ground to dig and plenty of cover
skunk.fact: A skunk would rather not spray you. First it stamps its front feet. Then it hisses. Then it does a handstand. Only if you ignore all three does it turn around and fire.
skunk.role: The forest's night gardener. At night it digs little cone-shaped holes across the forest floor looking for beetle grubs, and that turns the soil over as it goes. Almost nothing dares hunt it, except the great horned owl, which can barely smell.

towhee.diet: Bugs and small crawlers in summer. Seeds, acorns, and berries in winter
towhee.preferredHabitat: Brushy forest edges and scrub with deep leaf litter
towhee.fact: The spotted towhee feeds with a two-footed backward hop that flicks leaves aside.
towhee.role: The spotted towhee feeds on the ground and ties the bug layer to the seed layer. It eats ground beetles and caterpillars in summer and spreads seeds in winter. It nests on the ground, so foxes, raccoons, and snakes get the nests while hawks and owls take the adults. Its scratching turns over the leaf litter.

prairie-vole.fact: Voles mow narrow paths through the grass. They are tidy little roads they patrol between burrow doors.
prairie-vole.role: A tiny mouse that almost every hunter eats, and it has babies fast. It turns meadow plants into food for everyone else. Its eating and its little grass paths shape the grass layer. Hawks, owls, foxes, snakes, and badgers all count on it.

river-otter.fact: River otters can hold their breath for up to eight minutes while hunting.
river-otter.role: A quick swimmer that hunts fish and crayfish through the channels. Otters hold down fish and frog numbers. Seeing one means the water is clean and well linked.

muskrat.fact: Muskrats can stay under water for up to 15 minutes on one breath.
muskrat.role: A mostly plant-eating rodent that cuts reeds and cattails. That opens lanes of open water for ducks and other marsh life. Mink and otters eat it.

red-winged-blackbird.fact: Male red-winged blackbirds can hide their red shoulder patches. They flash them whenever they want.
red-winged-blackbird.role: A loud, common marsh bird that eats bugs and seeds. Males guard their reed patch hard. One patch may hold a dozen nests.

painted-turtle.fact: Painted turtles spend winter under the ice. They take in air through their skin.
painted-turtle.role: A turtle that suns itself, eats plants, and hunts bugs and small fish. It cleans up dead animals too. The young eat mostly meat and eat more plants as they grow.

chorus-frog.fact: A chorus frog’s call carries up to half a mile across the marsh.
chorus-frog.role: A tiny frog that eats small bugs. Its spring song fills the marsh. Herons, mink, and snakes all need it for food.

kit-fox.fact: The smallest wild dog in North America. Its huge ears hear prey and let out heat.
kit-fox.role: A small desert fox that hunts mice and rabbits at night. It hardly ever drinks, since it gets water from its food. Coyotes are its biggest danger.

mountain-lion.diet: deer and wild sheep mostly. Also jackrabbits, foxes, and anything it can get close to
mountain-lion.shelter: It has no fixed home. The kittens are hidden in a dry cave or under a rock ledge
mountain-lion.preferredHabitat: Broken canyon country with ledges, boulders, and brush to sneak through. It needs water too
mountain-lion.fact: The biggest cat out here cannot roar. It purrs like a house cat and screams like a nightmare. From standing still, it can jump five metres straight up onto a ledge.
mountain-lion.role: The top hunter of the desert. It does not chase. It sneaks up close, then explodes. So it needs rough ground and brush to hide in. Out on the open flat it goes hungry. It drags a big kill into cover and buries it under sticks and sand to come back to for days. That feeds ravens, foxes, and beetles too. Nothing out here hunts a grown one.
mountain-lion.hint: Big prey first. Then rough broken ground to sneak through and a sheltered ledge for the kittens. It does come down to drink.

kangaroo-rat.fact: Kangaroo rats never sweat or pant. They live on water made from the dry seeds they eat.
kangaroo-rat.role: A seed-eating desert rodent and key food animal. It buries seeds, which shapes which plants grow. Rattlesnakes, owls, and foxes all live on it.

jackrabbit.fact: A jackrabbit’s huge ears work like radiators. They let out body heat to keep it cool.

quail.fact: One male keeps watch from a perch while the rest of the group feeds below.
quail.role: A friendly ground bird that eats seeds, greens, and cactus fruit. Coyotes, bobcats, and desert hawks all need it for food. Flocks scratch through the brush together.

horned-lizard.fact: Texas horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes to startle a hunter.
horned-lizard.role: A lizard that eats mostly one kind of ant and has a big belly to hold them. Roadrunners, hawks, shrikes, and snakes hunt it.

desert-tarantula.fact: A desert desert tarantula may live 25 years, most of it within a few feet of one burrow.
desert-tarantula.role: A big spider that lives many years. At night it waits in its hole and grabs bugs and other small creatures. Birds, snakes, and wasps hunt it.

scorpion.fact: Scorpions glow blue-green under black light. Nobody is quite sure why.
scorpion.role: The biggest scorpion in North America. At night it waits and grabs bugs, spiders, and even other scorpions. Owls, snakes, and lizards eat it.

cactus-bee.fact: Cactus bees nest alone, but thousands of them share the same patch of ground.
cactus-bee.role: A bee that lives alone. It moves pollen for desert cactus like prickly pear and cholla. It eats nectar and pollen, and the cactus needs it to make fruit.

sea-star.fact: The classic key animal. Take it away and mussels take over the whole shore.
sea-star.role: The best-known key animal of the rocky shore. By eating mussels it sets how far down the mussel bed can grow. That leaves room for many other kinds of life.

anemone.fact: Its green glow comes from algae living inside it. The algae share the sugars they make.
anemone.role: A tidepool hunter that waits and grabs whatever the waves knock loose. It also grows tiny algae inside itself for extra food. It is a small hunter that helps clean up loose shellfish and crabs.

mussel.fact: One mussel cleans several liters of sea water an hour as it feeds.
mussel.role: A filter feeder that builds reefs. Its beds make homes for countless small animals. It is the key food that ties the top shore hunters together, from sea stars to sea otters to oystercatchers.

brown-pelican.fact: Brown pelicans dive from up to 65 feet, twisting to protect the neck as they hit.
brown-pelican.role: A fish hunter that dives from the air. It nearly died out from the pesticide DDT and then came back, which is one of the great wins for wildlife. Where pelicans are, the water holds healthy schools of small fish.

harbor-seal.fact: Harbor seals can sleep under water. They come up to breathe without fully waking.
harbor-seal.role: A sea hunter that eats whatever fish is easy to catch. Sharks and killer whales hunt it out at sea, but on this healed coast it sits near the top of the food web.

marsh-wren.fact: Males build many spare nests and even break their neighbours’ eggs.
marsh-wren.role: A tiny, feisty bug eater of the reeds. It picks bugs and spiders off the stems, and males build several fake nests to win a mate.

cactus-woodpecker.fact: The holes it leaves in cactus later shelter elf owls, tiny owls, and kestrels.
cactus-woodpecker.role: A woodpecker that nests in cactus and builds homes for the whole desert. It eats bugs, cactus fruit, and berries. Its old holes shelter many other animals. Hawks, snakes, and bobcats hunt it.

cactus-wren.fact: Cactus wrens use their ball-shaped nests all year, even for sleeping.
cactus-wren.role: The biggest wren in North America. It picks spiders and bugs off the brush and eats cactus fruit. It gets most of its water from its food. Snakes, roadrunners, and hawks take it and raid its nests.

sanderling.fact: Sanderlings chase the waves back out in busy little sprints to grab stranded creatures.
sanderling.role: A small sandpiper that chases the waves in and out, eating tiny sea bugs and worms the surf digs up. Falcons hunt it. Its winter flocks show how healthy open sandy beaches are.

puffin.fact: A puffin can hold a dozen fish crosswise in its beak without dropping any. Backward-pointing spines on its tongue and the roof of its mouth pin each fish while it catches the next.
puffin.role: A small seabird that spends almost its whole life out at sea. It only comes ashore to nest, and it digs a burrow into the turf on top of a cliff. Its beak only turns bright orange for the breeding season, then fades again for winter.

brant-goose.fact: Whole flocks of brant depend on eelgrass beds to fuel their long trips.
brant-goose.role: A small sea goose. It eats almost nothing but eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays. Since it needs eelgrass, healthy brant flocks mean the sea grass beds are whole.

snowy-plover.fact: Western snowy plovers nest in tiny scrapes right on the open sand.
snowy-plover.role: A beach-nesting bird that is at risk. It eats tiny animals along the sand and tide line. It is easily scared off its nest, so it only does well on quiet, protected dune beaches.

desert-hummingbird.fact: A male dives past a female with a high whistle. His purple throat flashes in the sun.
desert-hummingbird.role: A small desert hummingbird that drinks nectar from agave, chuparosa, and other blooms and eats tiny bugs. It moves lots of pollen. Snakes and hunting birds catch it.

phainopepla.fact: This bird spreads desert mistletoe seeds. The two depend on each other.
phainopepla.role: A shiny black desert bird that lives mostly on mistletoe berries in winter and catches bugs in the air. It is the main spreader of mistletoe seeds. Snakes and hawks hunt it.

antelope-squirrel.fact: It carries its tail arched over its back like a parasol for shade.

crow.role: The smartest bird on the shore. It walks the tide line looking for anything left stranded. It cracks open what it cannot bite through. It follows the gulls and the otters to see what they turn up.

mink.role: A bold hunter that swims after fish, frogs, and even muskrats. Mink are mid-sized hunters that help hold down small marsh animals.

mallard.role: A duck that tips head down to eat seeds, plants, and small water bugs. Its ducklings and eggs feed many marsh hunters.

sandhill-crane.role: A tall bird of the open marsh. It digs for roots and grain and snaps up bugs and small animals. When cranes are here, the wetland is wide and healthy.

merganser.role: A small diving duck. Its bill has saw-like teeth for holding slippery prey. It chases fish, crayfish, and bugs under water. It nests in tree holes.

roadrunner.role: A bird that runs down lizards, bugs, scorpions, and snakes on foot. It is a key hunter of small desert reptiles and bugs. Coyotes and hawks hunt it.

desert-tortoise.role: A plant eater that lives a very long time and builds homes for others. Its holes can run more than 10 metres and shelter snakes, lizards, mice, and bugs. Grown tortoises have thick shells, so few things can hurt them.

rattlesnake.role: A snake with venom that waits, then strikes. It is a big check on desert mouse numbers. It swallows prey whole and only needs to eat every few weeks. Roadrunners, hawks, and other snakes hunt it.

hermit-crab.role: A tidepool cleaner. It eats algae and dead animals. It moves into empty snail shells to stay safe. Gulls, fish, and octopus all eat it.

gull.role: A bold bird that eats almost anything. It cleans up dead animals and hunts crabs, shellfish, and even sea stars, which links many kinds of prey to the top of the food web. Foxes and coyotes take gulls and their eggs on land.

snow-flea.diet: Dead leaves and stems, fungus threads, pollen, and the pink algae that grows on old snow
snow-flea.shelter: Wet dead leaves, moss, and the gap between the snow and the ground in winter
snow-flea.preferredHabitat: Damp mountain grass, moss, and wet leaves. Also the top of old snow on warm days
snow-flea.fact: On a mild winter day, snow fleas pour onto the snow in their thousands. It looks like spilled pepper. Their blood is full of antifreeze, so they keep moving when everything else is frozen stiff.
snow-flea.role: The clean-up crew. Without them, last year's leaves would pile up forever. They chew dead stems and graze fungus threads into soil. They keep at it all winter, in the dark gap under the snow. Pipits, finches, chickadees, bluebirds, nutcrackers, and toads all eat them.
snow-flea.hint: A mat of dead leaves under melting snow. That is enough to start.

purple-sea-urchin.diet: Living kelp and surfgrass, loose kelp that drifts by, and hard pink algae on the rock
purple-sea-urchin.shelter: A pit it grinds into the rock with its own teeth and spines
purple-sea-urchin.preferredHabitat: Rock near kelp, low down the shore, with waves washing over it
purple-sea-urchin.fact: A purple urchin chews a pit into solid rock with five teeth. Then it sits in that pit for years. On some reefs, urchins wear away more stone than the waves do.
purple-sea-urchin.role: This grazer sits at the heart of the coast's most famous story. Otters keep their numbers down, and scraps of loose kelp keep them fed. Then they are just one more part of a healthy forest. Take the hunters away and they march up the rock. They mow the kelp down to bare stone and leave an empty desert behind.
purple-sea-urchin.hint: Kelp first. There has to be something to eat. Then think hard about what will keep the grazers in check.

anchovy.diet: Plankton: tiny animals, plant cells, and larvae, strained from the water or picked off one at a time
anchovy.shelter: The school itself. Open water near shore, with kelp and surfgrass edges as cover for the young
anchovy.preferredHabitat: Cool water near shore with plenty of plankton in it
anchovy.fact: An anchovy eats in two ways. It can snap at big prey one bite at a time. Or it can open its mouth and swim, straining the sea like a living net.
anchovy.role: Anchovies swim in silver schools so thick they turn the water dark from below. Almost every hunter here takes them at some point: pelicans, seals, dolphins, gulls. So when the anchovies fail, the whole coast goes hungry at once.
anchovy.hint: Cold water rising from the deep grows the plankton they eat. Quiet shallows give the schools a place to lay eggs.

beach-hopper.diet: Rotting kelp and other seaweed washed up at the tide line
beach-hopper.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high up the beach, and the wet underside of kelp and driftwood
beach-hopper.preferredHabitat: A gently sloping sandy beach with the seaweed left where it lands
beach-hopper.fact: Beach hoppers spend all day shut inside a burrow in dry sand. After dark they pour out to shred the seaweed the tide left behind. Step near one and it fires into the air like a flicked pebble.
beach-hopper.role: The engine room of the beach. Hoppers chew washed-up kelp down into crumbs. That turns dead seaweed into bird food, which is the whole reason plovers, sanderlings, and gulls walk the tide line. Rake the seaweed away and this link is gone overnight.
beach-hopper.hint: Leave the seaweed where the tide drops it. That is the whole meal.

desert-termite.diet: Dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung, and the weathered outside of dead wood
desert-termite.shelter: Tunnels and rooms underground, plus a mud roof built over whatever it is eating
desert-termite.preferredHabitat: Soil under shrubs and grass where dead leaves and stems pile up
desert-termite.fact: These termites spread a thin mud roof over a dead stem and eat under it. That way they can feed in full sun and never touch the dry air.
desert-termite.role: This is the animal that recycles the desert. There is too little water here for dead plants to rot the way they do in a forest. So termites eat almost all of it instead. They carry the goodness back underground. They also leave tunnels that let rain soak in instead of running off. On the nights they swarm, everything with a beak or a sting comes to feed.
desert-termite.hint: Bury a little dead wood and they will find it. Dead wood is the desert's pantry.

raven.diet: Dead animals most of all, plus eggs, chicks, young reptiles, bugs, and cactus fruit
raven.shelter: A big stick nest on a cliff or in a tall cactus. More and more often, on power poles
raven.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall places to nest and food it can count on
raven.fact: Ravens remember single human faces and hold the grudge for years. A pair will even run a trick together. One bird makes a fuss while the other steals the food.
raven.role: The clean-up crew, and the biggest human story in the desert. Roads, dumps, farms, and power poles hand ravens free food, water, and places to nest. So there are far more of them than this desert could ever feed on its own. All those extra ravens eat baby tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Cutting off the free meals is now a real part of saving the tortoise.
raven.hint: They follow whatever gets left lying around: a dead animal, a tall perch, something to drink. That is all they ask for, and that is the trouble.

polyphemus-moth.diet: tree leaves as a caterpillar. Oak, birch, maple and willow. The grown moth has no mouth and never eats
polyphemus-moth.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf. The cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and lies on the forest floor all winter
polyphemus-moth.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woods and woodland edges with oak, birch, and hickory, and deep leaves left lying below
polyphemus-moth.fact: The grown moth has no mouth. It cannot eat one single thing. Everything it will ever spend on finding a mate and laying eggs was eaten months before, by the caterpillar.
polyphemus-moth.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer. Nearly every forest bird depends on that step. Caterpillars turn tough, chewy tree leaves into soft protein. And it is caterpillars, not seeds, that woodland songbirds stuff into their chicks. The adults that make it feed bats at dusk. The cocoons spend all winter down in the fallen leaves. So a wood raked bare in autumn throws next summer's moths out with the leaf bags.
polyphemus-moth.hint: Broadleaf trees for the caterpillars to eat, and leaves left lying all winter for the cocoons hidden among them.

freshwater-shrimp.diet: Dead leaves and stems, the fungus and germs growing on them, and algae scraped off water plants
freshwater-shrimp.shelter: Among sunken dead leaves, plant stems, and the loose mud on top
freshwater-shrimp.preferredHabitat: Shallow water with plenty of air in it and a deep drift of rotting leaves
freshwater-shrimp.fact: Freshwater shrimp swim on their sides. Males carry females around piggyback for days before they mate. Lift a handful of soggy leaves out of a pond and dozens will be flicking about in it.
freshwater-shrimp.role: The marsh's shredder. One shrimp chews a single dead cattail leaf into thousands of crumbs. It is really after the fungus furring the leaf, not the leaf itself. That is how a heap of dead plants becomes food for minnows, young salamanders, and young dragonflies.
freshwater-shrimp.hint: A drift of rotting leaves in still water is all they need.

crayfish.diet: Rotting plants and dead animals, live water plants, snails, insect young, and freshwater shrimp
crayfish.shelter: Burrows dug into soggy banks, and gaps under sunken logs and stones
crayfish.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with sunken wood, and a bank soft enough to dig into
crayfish.fact: Lose a claw in a fight and a crayfish just grows a new one. It comes back bigger at every moult, until it matches the old one. Startle it and it flips its tail and shoots backwards, faster than you can grab.
crayfish.role: The marsh's recycler, and nearly everybody's dinner. Crayfish shred dead plants and clean up dead animals. That turns buried gunk back into living meat. Then the otter, the mink, the kingfisher, the merganser, the crane, the snapping turtle, and the heron come and take it.
crayfish.hint: A soft bank to tunnel into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plants to eat.

freshwater-mussel.diet: Algae, germs, and fine dead bits strained out of the water
freshwater-mussel.shelter: Buried upright in firm, fine mud with only its two tubes showing
freshwater-mussel.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand
freshwater-mussel.fact: A baby mussel has to hitch a ride. It clamps onto the gills of a passing fish and rides there for weeks. Then it drops off and starts life on the bottom. Some mother mussels even wave a flap of flesh shaped like a little fish to pull a host in close.
freshwater-mussel.role: The marsh's water filter, and one of the longest-lived animals in it. One mussel can strain the same patch of water for thirty years. What it catches drops to the bottom for shrimp and crayfish. No fish means no baby mussels. So they only come back after the minnows do.
freshwater-mussel.hint: A settled bed that stays put for years. And fish, because the young ride to their new home clamped to fish gills.

pillbug.diet: Dead leaves, rotting wood, dead grass, and fungus threads. Also droppings and old bones, for the minerals
pillbug.shelter: Hides by day under crumbling logs, flat stones, and deep leaves, where the air stays damp
pillbug.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners of the meadow with rotting wood and a thick layer of dead leaves
pillbug.fact: A pillbug is not an insect at all. It is a crustacean, closer kin to a crab than to a beetle. It still breathes through flaps like gills, and they have to stay wet.
pillbug.role: Pillbugs work the night shift under logs and dead grass. They shred dead leaves and soft rotten wood into crumbs. Fungus and germs can then finish the job. That is the first step in turning last year's meadow into next year's soil. Garter snakes and killdeer hunt them, so the clean-up crew feeds upward as well as downward.
pillbug.hint: Damp, dark, and rotting is the whole recipe. A crumbling log, deep dead grass, and ground that never dries right out. Roll one over and it curls into a ball.

garden-spider.diet: Flying and jumping bugs caught in the web: grasshoppers, bees, flies, and moths
garden-spider.shelter: Hangs head-down in the middle of its own round web, strung between tall stems
garden-spider.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow with tall stiff plants left standing and plenty of flying bugs
garden-spider.fact: This spider takes most of its web down every night and eats the old silk to build the next one. It also stitches a bold white zigzag through the middle, and nobody has fully worked out why.
garden-spider.role: The meadow's trapper. It slings a wheel of silk wider than your hand between tall stems. Then it waits head-down in the middle for grasshoppers, bees, and flies to blunder in. Spiders are the biggest group of hunters in any grassland. They were also the biggest thing missing from this meadow until now. They eat huge numbers of bugs, and they are the main food of half the songbirds here.
garden-spider.hint: Tall stiff stems left standing, far enough apart to sling a big web between them, with flowers close by to bring the bugs in.

brown-bat.diet: Bugs that fly at night, mostly beetles, plus moths, flying ants, and midges
brown-bat.shelter: Sleeps by day in warm dark spaces: barn lofts, attics, and under loose bark. Winters in cold cracks
brown-bat.preferredHabitat: Open air over meadow and hedges to hunt in, still water to drink from, and a warm sleeping spot nearby
brown-bat.fact: A big brown bat finds a moth in total darkness by shouting and listening to the echo. It can pick out something no thicker than a pencil lead this way.
brown-bat.role: The night shift over the meadow. These bats work the air above the grass and along the hedges after sunset. They catch beetles, moths, and flying ants. One bat can eat thousands of bugs in a single night. They drink on the wing, dipping their jaws into still water without stopping. Mothers gather in warm roosts to raise pups together. Great horned owls catch them at dusk.
brown-bat.hint: A warm crack to raise pups in, bugs in the air above the grass, and calm open water to skim a drink from without landing.

snail.diet: Dead leaves, soft rotting stems, and the algae film on damp stones
snail.shelter: Seals itself to the underside of a damp log or stone and waits out dry weather
snail.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners with dead leaves and something chalky to scrape at
snail.fact: A snail carries its own house and can shut the door behind it. When things get dry it glues itself to a stone and sleeps until it rains. Sometimes that takes months.
snail.role: Snails are the meadow's slow recyclers. They shred fallen leaves into crumbs that fungus and soil life can finish off. When they die, their shells give calcium back to the ground.
snail.hint: A shady damp corner where leaves are left to pile up and rot. The messy bit is the point here, not the tidy bit.

wolverine.diet: marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan when it can catch them. Frozen dead animals when it cannot. Berries in late summer
wolverine.shelter: Tunnels dug metres down into deep spring snow, usually beside a fallen boulder or log, with food stored in side rooms
wolverine.preferredHabitat: Big, empty, high country with broken rock, and snow that lasts into late spring
wolverine.fact: A wolverine can smell a dead animal buried under three metres of snow, dig it out, and then drive a bear off it. It does all that in a body about the size of a small dog.
wolverine.role: The biggest weasel in the world, and the mountain's great scavenger. It is now the top hunter on these peaks. It roams huge distances. It kills marmots, hares, and white-tailed ptarmigan when it gets the chance, and lives off frozen dead animals when it does not. Its jaws are built to crack frozen bone. Snow is its fridge. It stores food in drifts and dens deep inside them. So a female can only raise young where the snow holds into late spring. That makes it the first animal to go when winters get short. And nothing up here will argue with it over a dead animal.
wolverine.hint: What is needed here is space and snow, not views. Drifts deep enough to last into late spring, for the den and the food store. Broken rock to travel through. And marmots and hares already on the mountain.

bottlenose-dolphin.diet: Fish that swim in schools, above all anchovy, plus squid and fish from the bottom
bottlenose-dolphin.shelter: It builds none. It sleeps at sea in a small group. Half its brain stays awake
bottlenose-dolphin.preferredHabitat: Water close in along an open beach, with strong surf and fish schools offshore
bottlenose-dolphin.fact: Every dolphin makes up its own whistle. The others copy that whistle back when they want to call it over. Along an open beach, these dolphins hunt right inside the breaking waves they are herding fish against.
bottlenose-dolphin.role: Fast, sociable hunters that work the surf in small groups. They push anchovy schools up against the breaking waves until the fish have nowhere left to go. They are quick and clever enough to catch almost anything that schools here. And they are still not the biggest thing in the water.
bottlenose-dolphin.hint: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and real breaking surf, because that is where the hunting happens.

orca.diet: Sea mammals: harbor seals most of all, plus dolphins, sea lions, and gray whale calves
orca.shelter: None on land. It rests at the surface in deep water with its family
orca.preferredHabitat: Cold deep water close to shore, where the sea floor drops away by the kelp edge, within reach of seal resting rocks
orca.fact: Orcas live in families that never split up, and different families eat completely different food. The ones that hunt this coast eat only mammals. They go silent to do it, with no clicks and no calls, because a seal can hear a talking orca coming from a long way off.
orca.role: The top of this coast, with nothing above it. A family of mammal-hunting orcas patrols the edge where the sea floor drops away. They listen at seal rocks. In spring they shadow gray whales passing through with calves. When they come into a bay, every seal on the rocks goes still and silent.
orca.hint: Deep water pressed right up against the shore, and something big to hunt. Bring the seals back first, because the seals are the whole draw.

desert-millipede.diet: Dead leaves, stems, seed husks, and other dry plant litter on the ground
desert-millipede.shelter: Buried in soil and tucked under leaves and flat rocks by day; out walking on damp nights
desert-millipede.preferredHabitat: Drifts of dead leaves under shrubs, with flat rocks and soft soil nearby
desert-millipede.fact: A desert millipede spends most of the year underground. Then it pours out by the hundreds after the first summer storm. Touch one and it coils into a tight spiral like a cinnamon bun. It also oozes a bitter brown liquid that stains your fingers for days.
desert-millipede.role: The litter shredder. It chews dead leaves, stems, and husks into crumbs. Termites and tiny soil life can then finish the job. That is how dead plants become soil again out here. It has hundreds of legs and no hurry at all. Armor and a foul chemical mean it can afford to stroll. Scorpions and roadrunners eat it anyway.
desert-millipede.hint: Let the leaves drift up under the shrubs, and leave a flat rock to crawl beneath. Damp leaves are both dinner and hiding place. Bare hot sand is neither.

desert-hawk.diet: Jackrabbits, ground squirrels, quail, woodrats, and lizards
desert-hawk.shelter: A big stick nest wedged in the arms of a tall cactus or a thorny tree, built and guarded by the whole family
desert-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open scrub with tall cactus and trees to nest in and watch from
desert-hawk.fact: These are the only birds of prey in the world that hunt in packs. A family of five or six spreads out. Some crash into a thorn bush to panic a rabbit while the others wait on the far side. And when there is nowhere good to perch, they stand on each other's backs, three birds high.
desert-hawk.role: The top hunter by day. It works the same desert the mountain lion works at night. Two or three generations live together all year. They share every kill, help feed each other's chicks, and take turns on lookout. That teamwork lets them bring down jackrabbits far heavier than one bird could handle alone. They need tall lookouts above open ground, and a big cactus strong enough to hold a family nest.
desert-hawk.hint: One bird is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.

bald-eagle.diet: mostly fish. Also ducks, muskrats and dead animals. It robs other hunters too
bald-eagle.shelter: A huge stick nest in the top of the tallest living tree beside open water, added to every year
bald-eagle.preferredHabitat: Wide open water full of fish, with one very tall tree to watch it all from
bald-eagle.fact: A bald eagle would rather rob than fish. It follows otters and herons and pesters them until they drop their catch, then takes it. The nest it rebuilds every year can end up heavier than a small car.
bald-eagle.role: The top hunter of the marsh, and its biggest bully. It takes fish, ducks, and muskrats for itself. It kills herons at their nesting colonies. It spends much of the day stealing meals from otters and herons. So it can only settle somewhere those hunters are already doing well.
bald-eagle.hint: One huge old tree with a clear view over deep water. Enough fish to live on. And otters and herons below doing well enough to steal from.

luna-moth.diet: Hickory, walnut, sweetgum, and birch leaves as a caterpillar. The grown moth eats nothing at all
luna-moth.shelter: A papery cocoon spun inside a curled leaf. The leaf falls, and the cocoon lies buried in the dead leaves all winter
luna-moth.preferredHabitat: Old broadleaf woods with deep dead leaves left alone under the trees
luna-moth.fact: A grown luna moth has no mouth. It comes out with about a week to live. It never eats once, and it spends that whole week looking for a mate.
luna-moth.role: Luna moth caterpillars eat leaves and turn them into fat, high-energy insect bodies. Everything from bats to jays cashes that in. The long twisted tails on the back wings are an anti-bat trick. They spin as the moth flies and throw a bat's echo off target. So the bat grabs a tail streamer instead of the body. The cocoon spends winter in the fallen leaves. So a forest that gets raked loses its luna moths, even if every tree is still standing.
luna-moth.hint: Plant the leafy trees, then let the leaves lie where they fall. The cocoons spend the whole winter down in them.

blue-jay.diet: Acorns and beechnuts, caterpillars, beetles and other bugs, and eggs or chicks when it finds them
blue-jay.shelter: A cup of twigs and roots wedged in a fork high in a leafy tree, hidden by the leaves
blue-jay.preferredHabitat: Woods full of oaks, and their edges, with open ground nearby for burying acorns
blue-jay.fact: Blue jay feathers are not really blue. The color in them is brown. The blue is a trick of light bouncing off tiny air pockets. Crush one and the blue is gone.
blue-jay.role: One blue jay can carry five acorns at a time and bury a few thousand in one autumn. It picks the sound ones and pushes them into open ground.
