That makes jays the fastest tree planters in the forest, and the reason oaks spread uphill after a fire. Jays also copy hawk calls. Sometimes that clears a feeding spot. Sometimes it warns everything nearby that a real hawk has arrived. So the whole wood listens to them.
blue-jay.hint: Oaks, and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some get forgotten. Those are your next oak trees.

wood-frog.diet: Beetles, spiders, slugs, flies, and other small creatures from the forest floor
wood-frog.shelter: Shallow dead leaves and loose litter on the forest floor. It does not dig down below the frost
wood-frog.preferredHabitat: Damp broadleaf forest with fishless woodland pools that fill in spring and dry up by late summer
wood-frog.fact: A wood frog freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops. Two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice. In spring it thaws out and hops away.
wood-frog.role: Wood frogs are the first frog to call in spring. They breed in pools that dry up before fish can ever live in them. That is exactly why the tadpoles survive. Sugar floods their blood and stops their cells bursting while they are frozen. So they can sleep the winter under a few centimetres of leaves. Grown frogs eat their way through the small creatures in the dead leaves. Snakes and raccoons then eat them, which carries food up the chain.
wood-frog.hint: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind. No fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby to freeze in.

goshawk.diet: Squirrels, jays, grouse, rabbits, and woodpeckers, chased down inside the trees
goshawk.shelter: A wide stick nest against the trunk on a heavy branch, halfway up a big old tree
goshawk.preferredHabitat: Old forest with a high closed roof of leaves and open flying room under it
goshawk.fact: A goshawk hunts by crashing straight through the branches at full speed with its wings half folded. It will dive at anything that walks too near its nest, people included.
goshawk.role: The forest's top hunter by day, and the reason squirrels freeze against tree trunks. Short wide wings and a long steering tail let it turn inside a wood at speed. So it hunts under the leaves, not above them like a soaring hawk. It needs old forest with big branches to nest on, and clear space below to fly. That is why its arrival means the trees have finally grown up.
goshawk.hint: Grow the forest tall and leave the space below it open. A big branch to nest on, and room to fly hard under the leaves.

moose.diet: Pondweed and water lilies in summer, willow and aspen twigs in winter
moose.shelter: Beds pressed into willow thickets. In summer it stands chest-deep in water to escape the flies
moose.preferredHabitat: Marsh and pond edge with thick willow and clear shallow water
moose.fact: A moose can hold its breath for a minute and walk along the bottom of a pond with its whole head under water, pulling plants up by the roots.
moose.role: Moose come to the wetland for salt. The underwater plants have it and forest leaves do not. A big one can pull 20 kilograms of pondweed a day out of the shallows. All that heavy feeding keeps open lanes through the plant beds, where ducks feed and fish shelter. The willow it eats in winter grows back thicker and lower, which is better cover for everything small. Its trails through the marsh turn into channels that hold water in dry summers.
moose.hint: Grow the underwater plant beds first, and keep the water clear enough for them. The draw here is what grows under the surface, not on the bank.

river-cooter.diet: Pondweed, algae, water lily leaves, and fallen fruit. Babies eat bugs first, then switch to plants
river-cooter.shelter: Sleeps wedged under sunken logs and root tangles. Spends the winter buried in the mud at the bottom
river-cooter.preferredHabitat: Slow, plant-filled water with logs to bask on and an open sunny bank to lay eggs in
river-cooter.fact: Whether the eggs hatch into males or females depends on how warm the nest is, not on the eggs. A cool nest makes brothers. A warm one makes sisters.
river-cooter.role: This is the wetland's big plant-eating turtle. It crops the underwater meadows so they do not choke the shallows. It also drops the seeds somewhere else, still whole. It has to bask for hours to get warm enough to digest all that plant food. That is why a log stacked with turtles is a sign of a working marsh. Its eggs and babies feed almost everything else, so it lays a lot of them.
river-cooter.hint: Logs in the sun to bask on, and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. No warm spot means no way to digest dinner.

javelina.diet: Prickly pear pads, mesquite pods, agave hearts, roots, and tubers
javelina.shelter: The herd beds down in the shade of thick thorny scrub or under a rock ledge through the heat of the day
javelina.preferredHabitat: Desert scrub and dry washes with thick thorny cover and prickly pear
javelina.fact: A javelina eats prickly pear whole, spines and all. It also has a scent gland on its back so strong that a herd can find each other in the dark by smell alone.
javelina.role: Javelinas are the desert's cactus crushers. They crunch through pads that nothing else will touch, which stops prickly pear taking over a wash. They spread its seeds in their droppings too. Rooting for tubers turns over hard crusted soil and buries dead leaves, so seeds have somewhere to sprout after rain. They travel in herds of six to a dozen. The herd smell is also the alarm system, because their eyesight is terrible.
javelina.hint: Grow the prickly pear and leave a shady thorny tangle to bed down in. The herd sleeps out the middle of the day and feeds at dusk.

black-swift.diet: Flying ants, aphids, beetles, and mayflies caught in the air, often hundreds of metres up
black-swift.shelter: A cup of moss glued to wet rock behind a waterfall. Only reachable from the air
black-swift.preferredHabitat: Cliffs with cold running water and wide open sky above the treeline
black-swift.fact: A black swift can stay in the air for six months without landing once. It eats, drinks, and sleeps flying. The chick is left alone all day while its parents hunt bugs 50 km away.
black-swift.role: Swifts hoover up the swarms of bugs that rising air lifts onto the mountain. They carry that food back as one squashed pellet. One delivery a day is enough for a chick, because the load is packed so tight. The nest has to stay wet and out of reach. So these birds only turn up where a cliff crack has water running over it. They are among the very last summer visitors to arrive, and the first to leave for the Amazon.
black-swift.hint: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. Nothing will nest here if it can be walked to.

peregrine-falcon.diet: Other birds, caught in mid-air: white-tailed ptarmigan, rosy-finches, swifts, pipits, and small ducks
peregrine-falcon.shelter: A bare dip kicked into gravel on a high cliff ledge. It builds no nest at all
peregrine-falcon.preferredHabitat: Steep cliffs and rock faces above open ground, with plenty of birds flying below
peregrine-falcon.fact: A diving peregrine hits about 380 km/h. That makes it the fastest animal alive. It has bony cones in its nostrils that slow the air down, so the dive does not burst its lungs.
peregrine-falcon.role: The mountain's hunter of the air. It takes almost all of its food in flight, striking from above with a closed fist instead of grabbing. It hunts birds and nothing else. So it is a direct check on the flocks of finches, pipits, and white-tailed ptarmigan feeding across the slopes. It needs a quiet cliff ledge and clear air below. It needs nothing at all to build with, just loose gravel to scrape a hollow in.
peregrine-falcon.hint: A high ledge with loose gravel on it, and open sky underneath. Do not build a nest. All it takes is a dip kicked in the grit.

sand-dollar.diet: Algae, plankton, and scraps of food picked out of the sand, grain by grain
sand-dollar.shelter: Half buried on edge in rippled sand, in beds of hundreds at a time
sand-dollar.preferredHabitat: Sheltered sandy bottoms just below the low tide line, where the current is gentle
sand-dollar.fact: A living sand dollar is not white and smooth. It is purple, and covered in tiny moving spines. It uses them to walk and to pass food along to its mouth. The white disc with the flower pattern is the skeleton, after everything else has washed away.
sand-dollar.role: A whole bed of them stands half buried on edge, like coins in a slot. They all lean into the current to catch what drifts past. Where the water is rougher, they lie flat instead, so they do not get rolled away.
sand-dollar.hint: Clean rippled sand just below the tide line, somewhere sheltered enough that the current stays gentle.

octopus.diet: Shore crabs, clams, mussels, snails, and shrimp, cracked open or drilled through
octopus.shelter: A crack or an empty shell, with a rock pulled across behind it and a heap of empty shells outside the door
octopus.preferredHabitat: Rocky sea floor and deep tidepools with lots of cracks and cold, clean water
octopus.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and it tastes everything it touches with its arms. The only hard part of it is its beak. So one the size of a dinner plate can squeeze through a hole the size of a grape.
octopus.role: The top hunter without a backbone on the rocky shore. The pile of empty crab and clam shells outside its den is the easiest way to find one. It can change color and skin texture in under a second to vanish against rock or kelp, even though it is colorblind. If a clam will not open, it drills a neat hole and puts in a drug that makes the shell relax. Each octopus works through a huge number of crabs, which keeps the grazers and cleaners of the tidepools in check.
octopus.hint: Broken rock with gaps to hide in, and plenty of crabs. Leave the shell pile outside the den alone. That pile is how you know somebody is home.

grasshopper-mouse.diet: Scorpions, centipedes, beetles, and other mice
grasshopper-mouse.shelter: Takes over a burrow another animal dug, then defends it
grasshopper-mouse.preferredHabitat: Open sandy flats with scattered brush and plenty of prey underfoot
grasshopper-mouse.fact: This mouse hunts scorpions, gets stung in the face, and carries on eating. Its body switches the venom's pain signal off. Then it stands up on its back legs and howls at the moon like a tiny wolf.
grasshopper-mouse.role: A mouse that decided to be a hunter. It keeps scorpions and big bugs in check. It is one of the only animals that can eat the most venomous creatures in the desert without flinching.
grasshopper-mouse.hint: An old burrow it can take over, and open ground to hunt across. It gets all its water from what it catches.

snow-bunting.diet: Seeds blown onto the snow, plus bugs in the short summer
snow-bunting.shelter: Deep in a crack in the rock, lined with feathers and fur against the cold
snow-bunting.preferredHabitat: Windswept ridges and stony ground where the snow blows clear
snow-bunting.fact: Snow buntings nest further north than any other songbird on Earth. They tuck so deep into rock cracks that the male has to feed the female in the dark while she sits on the eggs.
snow-bunting.role: A small bird that treats a blizzard as ordinary weather. Flocks drift across bare ridges, picking up seed the wind has stranded on the snow. They turn from white to warm brown as the season turns.
snow-bunting.hint: A deep, dry crack in the rock out of the wind, and open stony ground nearby where the snow blows clear.

groundhog.diet: Grass, clover, dandelions, and just about any soft green thing it can reach
groundhog.shelter: A burrow with several doors, a sleeping room lined with grass, and a separate toilet room
groundhog.preferredHabitat: Meadow edges with deep, well-drained soil it can dig through
groundhog.fact: A groundhog digs a burrow with a front door, a back door, a bedroom, and a separate room for the toilet. It moves about a tonne of soil doing it. In winter its heart slows to about five beats a minute.
groundhog.role: The meadow's earthmover. Its old burrows become homes for foxes, snakes, rabbits, and half the small animals here. So one groundhog's digging lasts for years after the digger has gone.
groundhog.hint: Deep, well-drained soil at the edge of the grass, with a bolt-hole close by. It wants a place to dig more than a place to hide.

opossum.diet: Almost anything: bugs, fruit, eggs, dead animals, and a huge number of ticks
opossum.shelter: Sleeps the day in a hollow log or a borrowed burrow. It rarely uses the same one twice
opossum.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges with hollow wood, water nearby, and plenty to scavenge
opossum.fact: When an opossum plays dead, it is not acting. It faints. The body goes stiff, the tongue lolls out, and it gives off a smell like something long dead. It cannot snap out of it for several minutes, even if you walk away.
opossum.role: The meadow's clean-up crew. It eats what everything else has left, including dead animals and huge numbers of ticks. It is the only animal here that carries its young around on its back.
opossum.hint: Hollow wood to sleep the day away in, and berries within a night's walk. It moves house all the time, so give it more than one option.

coyote.diet: Voles, rabbits, and ground squirrels; young deer; also fruit, bugs, and dead animals
coyote.shelter: Raises pups in a den dug into a brushy bank, often an old badger or fox hole made bigger
coyote.preferredHabitat: Open grassland and edges with brushy cover for a den, and water close by
coyote.fact: Three coyotes can sound like a dozen. Each one slides its voice up and down as it howls. So a small family throws up a wall of sound. Scientists call it the 'beau geste' trick.
coyote.role: The top hunter of this meadow, and the one that copes with anything. It hunts voles and rabbits alone. It hunts young deer in pairs. In between it eats fruit, bugs, and dead animals. Its return finally puts pressure on the foxes, badgers, and deer that nothing else here could touch. It will even trail a digging badger and grab whatever bolts out the far side.
coyote.hint: A brushy bank for a den, wide grass full of rabbits and voles, and water close by. It only moves in where there is already plenty to eat.

unlock.label: Bring Willow Meadow to 60% health. Welcome 10 meadow animals. Craft a Forest Restoration Kit.

forest.restorationGoal: Grow back the low plants, raise nesting trees and dead wood, and welcome the forest animals home.

unlock.label: Bring Old Hollow Forest to 80% health with 10 forest animals back. Welcome 25 animals in all. Craft a Wetland Restoration Kit.

wetland.restorationGoal: Bring back shallow water, reed beds, and mud banks so wetland life can return.

unlock.label: Bring Rushwater Wetland to 80% health with 13 wetland animals back. Welcome 45 animals in all. Craft a Scrubland Restoration Kit.

desert.description: A desert flat eaten down to bare ground. With no brush and no burrows, the heat keeps everything away.
desert.restorationGoal: Plant cactus and brush, build shade and burrows, and bring the desert back to life.

unlock.label: Bring Redstone Scrubland to 80% health with 15 desert animals back. Welcome 65 animals in all. Craft an Alpine Restoration Kit.

alpine.restorationGoal: Bring back mountain grass and snowmelt pools. Add rocky shelter for the animals up high.

unlock.label: Bring Graywind Heights to 80% health with 17 alpine animals back. Welcome 85 animals in all. Craft a Migration Path Marker.

coastal.description: A worn stretch of coast where the open sea breaks on the east edge. The dunes washed out and the tidepools are empty. Sea glass, kelp, coral, and the odd pearl still wash up.
coastal.restorationGoal: Hold the dunes in place, bring back tidepools and kelp, and open the shore to coast life again.

meadow.description: A meadow beside your home that used to bloom. Now it is dusty and quiet. The native grasses were stripped out, and the bugs that fed on them left too.
meadow.restorationGoal: Plant grass and wild flowers. Add water and shelter. Help 10 meadow animals come back.

welcome-grasshopper.flavor: You did it. You gathered, built, shaped the land, and welcomed your first neighbor. One hop in the grass, and you already know how to bring back a whole meadow.
welcome-grasshopper.hint: Every caretaker starts with one small arrival.

forager.hint: Gather, and keep gathering. Build a real pile.

makers-hands.hint: Keep crafting. One item will not heal a meadow.

green-thumb.flavor: Ten living things in soil you got ready yourself. Half of this work is just patience with a watering can.

meadow-first-bloom.hint: Grow the meadow well past its first lonely guest.

meadow-pollinators.flavor: Monarch, bumblebee, leafcutter, ladybug, painted lady. They work for free. They turn flowers into seeds, and seeds into more meadow.

meadow-apex.flavor: A fox only stays where there are voles and rabbits to hunt. So when it shows up, everything below it is finally fed.

meadow-reborn.flavor: Every animal that belongs here is home. The meadow does not need you to hum anymore. But it remembers who started it.

forest-understory.flavor: Ferns, shrubs, a squirrel arguing with a woodpecker, newts under the dead wood. A forest is built from the ground up, not the top down.

forest-reborn.flavor: From a cut-over hush to a full forest. Three layers, and every wing in between.

wetland-first-water.flavor: Shape the water and the water brings its own crowd. Frogs, water striders, dragonflies skating the top, a heron in the shallows.

wetland-engineer.hint: Welcome the one who builds homes for everyone else.

wetland-lakemaker.flavor: Enough open water to hold a sky. Turtles sun themselves, ducks dive, and the marsh has a center again.
wetland-lakemaker.hint: Open enough water, all in one piece, to hold a sky.

wetland-restored.flavor: Reeds where there was cracked mud. Channels that really flow. A wetland cleans all the water that leaves it, and asks for nothing.

desert-burrows.flavor: In the desert, the good spots are underground. A tortoise digs a burrow and an owl takes the spare room. Nobody wastes a hole here.

desert-hunter.flavor: A hunter that can wait out the heat means there is finally enough prey to wait for.

desert-reborn.flavor: The hardest land here, fully alive. From the elf owl in the cactus to the desert-tarantula under the stone.

alpine-haypile.flavor: The pika spends all summer stacking little hay piles for a winter it refuses to sleep through. Tiny animal, huge work ethic.
alpine-haypile.hint: Welcome back the little hay stacker of the rocks.

alpine-reborn.flavor: Goat to white-tailed-ptarmigan to trout in the snowmelt. The whole high country, brought back against the wind.

coastal-keystone.flavor: The classic key animal. Take the sea star away and mussels take everything. Put it back and the whole tidepool shares the rock again.
coastal-keystone.hint: Bring back the one animal that holds the tidepool together.

coastal-otter.flavor: Otters eat the urchins that eat the kelp. So an otter on the water means a forest under it. Few animals do more with a full belly.

coastal-reborn.flavor: From whale spouts to clams. The last and wildest stretch of the preserve, complete.

well-stocked.flavor: A thousand fallen things gathered. You stopped scraping by long ago. This is a real store.

master-builder.hint: Place homes until the whole preserve shows your hand.

master-gardener.flavor: Seventy-five living things put in the ground, one sprout at a time. This work is mostly just showing up with a watering can.

landscaper.hint: Shape soil and water across the preserve, over and over.

fully-equipped.hint: Take your basket, shovel, and watering can to the top.

naturalist.flavor: Every guide filled in. Every animal known. You do not just host wildlife now. You understand it.

recipe-collector.flavor: Seventy-five different things, each built at least once. You have used almost every tool on the bench.
recipe-collector.hint: Build a little of almost everything on the bench.

full-house.flavor: A hundred kinds of neighbor. The preserve is not healing anymore. It is thriving.

field-notes.hint: Watch your wild neighbors, again and again, all over.

three-restored.flavor: Three broken places, brought most of the way home. The preserve is tipping from healing to healed.

caretaker-of-the-whole.flavor: Every animal in every area is home. The broken land you found is now, simply, wild. The rarest star there is.

willow-tree.description: The tree this place is named for, grown from a watered bed.

small-pond.description: A clay-lined pond. Clean drinking water changes everything.

fern-spring.description: A mossy wet spot ringed with ferns. Damp ground wakes up the whole forest floor.

wooden-bridge.description: A strong plank bridge. Put it on open water to cross rivers and lakes.

mud-bank.description: A soft shaped bank for digging and sunning. Needs the restoration shovel.

burrow-mound.description: A starter bank for diggers. Needs the restoration shovel.

kelp-wrack.description: A safe line of washed-up kelp. A feast for the whole beach.

coastal-nesting-area.description: A roped-off quiet strip of upper beach for nesting.

coral-garden.description: Moved coral pieces that grow back into a living reef. Food and shelter for the whole shore.

sea-glass-lantern.description: Beach glass set in driftwood. It throws soft sea-green light at dusk.

pearl-display.description: A polished shell stand showing the rarest pearls the shore gives up.

sea-glass-path.description: Smooth sea glass pressed into the sand. A shiny path that keeps boots off the dunes.

small-chest.description: A woven and wood chest. Holds 120 materials. Anything in here can be used for crafting from anywhere.

field-journal-stand.description: A little stand for your journal. Read it wherever you put one.

wetland-restoration-kit.description: Liners, filters, and channel tools. Everything you need to bring water back. Making it helps open Rushwater Wetland.

forest-restoration-kit.description: Seed mixes, twine, and trail tools to open the grown-over forest path. Making it helps open Old Hollow Forest.

scrubland-restoration-kit.description: Sleds and tough cuttings to carry this work into the dry scrubland. Making it helps open Redstone Scrubland.

trail-signpost.description: A hand-painted sign to guide visitors through the preserve.

gazebo.description: An open shelter with a roof. A pretty centerpiece and a shady place to watch from.

fern-grove.description: Shady arching ferns that carpet the forest floor.

alder-snag.description: A dead alder left standing. A perch and a nest hole above the water.

ocotillo.description: Whip-like stalks with red tips. Cover and nectar in the open flats.

heather-mat.description: A low mountain mat of heather flowers above the rocks.

daisy-patch.description: Bright white daisies that open with the morning sun.

bulrush.description: Tall bulrushes with brown velvet heads along the bank.

gentian-patch.description: Bright blue mountain gentians, kept low by the wind.

bald-cypress.description: A tall swamp cypress with feathery needles and a wide, knobby base.

desert-ironwood.description: A dense, slow-growing tree. It shelters young plants in the open desert.

quaking-aspen.description: White-barked aspen whose golden leaves shake in the mountain wind.

flower-cart.description: A little wooden cart spilling over with cut flowers.

hammock.description: A woven hammock hung between two posts for lazy afternoons.

flower-pots.description: A neat row of clay pots full of blooms.

dew-basin.description: A shallow clay bowl that catches dew and rain. Precious desert water.

lichen-boulder.description: A weathered boulder crusted with lichen. Slow mountain grazing and a foothold for new life.

scree-slope.description: A shifting slope of broken rock, laced with the runways and hideouts of the high country.

juniper-thicket.description: A low, tough juniper heavy with frosted berries. Cover and winter food where little else grows.

cliff-nest-niche.description: A sheltered gap in the cliff, mossy and tucked away for high country nesters.

crystal-spring.description: An ice-cold spring rising through quartz. The purest, coldest water up here.

summit-prayer-flags.description: A bright line of worn flags strung between stone piles, snapping in the wind.

obsidian-totem.description: A polished column of volcanic glass that catches the high light like dark, still water.

large-chest.description: A big iron-banded chest. Holds 500 materials. Your main store.

home-bed.description: A comfy bed for resting between days of work.

home-armchair.description: A soft armchair to sink into after a long day.

home-lamp.description: A soft floor lamp for cozy evenings inside.

rain-basin.description: A carved stone bowl that catches rain. A drinking spot for visiting animals.

sunstone-cairn.description: A stack of sun-baked stones that hold the day heat into the evening.

frostflower-planter.description: A planter of pale ice-blooms that keep their shape long after the snow goes.

frostflower-vase.description: A glass vase of ice-blooms for the windowsill. They never wilt.

stormglass-chandelier.description: A hanging cluster of lightning-glass shards that spreads cool light across the room.

boardwalk.description: A raised plank path. Cross the marsh without stepping on the reeds and mud.

hiking-boots.description: Strong boots made from tough bark, springy moss, and woven reeds. Once made they are yours for good. Wear them to move a little faster.

grass-patch.description: A soft patch of new grass. A good first step for bare ground.

native-grass-patch.description: Native bunchgrass with roots deeper than the grass is tall. It holds the soil together and covers the ground all year.

wildflower-patch.description: A loose mix of wild flowers, planted in no set order. A wide splash of colour you can spot from far away.

poppy-patch.description: Field poppies, an old farm weed from Europe. They look lovely in a garden bed, but they are not a prairie plant.

sunflower-patch.description: Tall sunflowers, wild in North America, left standing all autumn. The seed heads dry hard on the stalk and stay put.

lupine-patch.description: Tall blue lupine spikes. They feed the soil as they bloom.

oak-tree.description: An oak grown from an acorn. It starts slow, then for years it does more good than any other tree you can plant.

pine-tree.description: A young pine grown from a cone. Green shelter in every season.

butterfly-flowers.description: A mixed bed of wild nectar flowers, in bloom from midsummer to autumn. Milkweed is its own plant now, so sow that one on its own.

pollinator-garden.description: A thick bed of flowers planned to bloom all season long. Nectar and pollen from the first warm week to the last.

shrub.description: A young wild shrub that gives thick cover at knee height. But a meadow is grassland, and too many shrubs change it into something else.

berry-bush.description: A prickly thicket of wild rose and thimbleberry. It is full of fruit by late summer, so sow it in a watered bed.

woodland-pool.description: A shady forest pool fed by a cold spring. It is cold and clean, with a soft muddy edge to walk down.

shallow-water-pool.description: A pool with a long, sunny shallow edge you could wade across. It is warm and shallow, not deep, so it is no match for real deep water.

log-shelter.description: Fallen logs stacked in a loose pile with gaps running through it. It stays damp underneath and slowly goes soft.

hollow-log.description: A fallen log opened out down the middle. Inside is a dry, close space with one way in.

rock-pile.description: Flat stones piled loosely. The sun bakes the top while the gaps under it stay cool and damp.

fallen-branch-shelter.description: A loose heap of branches, twigs and all, thrown together rather than stacked. It is full of gaps to slip into.

bird-perch.description: A tall bare dead tree with a clear view all around. Open sky sits above it.

simple-path.description: Flat stepping stones that keep your boots off the new growth.

gravel-path.description: Crunchy gravel underfoot. It keeps boots off the new growth.

plank-path.description: Old boardwalk planks. They are gentle on soft ground.

flagstone-path.description: Wide flat stones set into the ground.

mossy-path.description: Old stones wearing soft green moss. They keep boots off the wet ground without packing it down.

wooden-fence.description: A low rail fence. It marks quiet spots where the ground is healing.

nesting-tree.description: A young native tree that grows fast. Give it a few seasons and its top will be strong enough to hold weight.

standing-deadwood.description: A dead tree left standing and held safe. The thicker it is the better, since a thin stub cannot hold much.

mushroom-log.description: A damp, mossy log seeded with fungus. The fungus eats the wood and turns the dead log into food, soil, and shelter.

reed-bed.description: Thick reeds standing in shallow water. They grow tall enough to walk in and lose sight of the bank.

nesting-platform.description: A raised, quiet platform out in the open, flat on top with nothing above it. It does not take the place of a tree hole, a bank tunnel, or a big shared nest.

cattail-stand.description: Tall cattails crowded along the water's edge. They are thick at the base and shade the shallows behind them.

marsh-log.description: A half-sunk log with one end in the sun and the other under water. Dark, tight gaps run beneath it the whole way.

lily-pool.description: Still, clean water covered edge to edge with lily pads. The water under them stays cool and shady.

cactus-patch.description: Moved-in pad and barrel cactus. Fruit, water, and a spiny fort in one, though it is too short to hold a hole.

desert-brush.description: A mixed stand of low bursage and brittlebush. It is the small scrub that fills the gaps between bigger shrubs.

shaded-rock-shelter.description: Stacked slabs with a cool dark gap. Shelter from the midday sun.

alpine-wildflower-patch.description: Tough little mountain flowers, low and tight to the ground. They all bloom at once in the short summer, so this is food, not shelter.

snowmelt-pool.description: A stone pool that holds cold, clear snowmelt. Leave it empty, since water this high starts out bare.

tidepool.description: A rocky pool that keeps a bit of sea behind when the tide goes out. It is only a bit, so it warms up and goes salty.

dune-grass.description: Wild dunegrass that holds blowing sand. It grows in open, patchy clumps, not a thick wall.

driftwood-shelter.description: Old driftwood stacked into a shelter on the beach.

tide-chime.description: Shells and sea glass strung on driftwood. They ring softly in the sea breeze.

flower-vase.description: A clay pot of meadow flowers to brighten your camp.

migration-path-marker.description: Stone stacks and markers that make the high route safe again. Making it helps open Pelican Shore.

alpine-restoration-kit.description: Shade cloth, water stores, and climbing gear for the high country. Making it helps open Graywind Heights.

stone-lantern.description: A little stone lantern with a warm glow to light the path.

wooden-bench.description: An old bench turned silver by salt and sun. A quiet place to sit and just look.

garden-arch.description: A flowery arch over a path, heavy with blooms by midsummer. It is pretty, but it is a garden piece and nothing here needs one.

bird-bath.description: A shallow stone bowl on a stand, no deeper than a thumb. The bottom is rough for footing and the water is fresh.

planter-box.description: A wooden box planted with desert plants. Brittlebush, penstemon, and globemallow, not garden flowers.

clover-patch.description: Clover and trefoil brought in from away, soft and green underfoot. It crowds out wild flowers, so treat it as a garden patch, not real healing.

brush-pile.description: A loose pile of branches, thickest at the bottom and open in the middle. Gaps and runs lead in at ground level.

tree-stump.description: A mossy old stump full of holes and soft rot. It crumbles a little further into the ground every year.

sedge-tussock.description: Clumps of sedge standing in the shallows. Each one is a thick, knee-high tuft with dry footing inside.

agave-rosette.description: A spiny rosette that stays low for years. Then it throws up one flower stalk taller than you.

krummholz-pine.description: A dwarf pine bent by the wind. Rare shelter at the tree line.

eelgrass-bed.description: Eelgrass swaying in soft mud in a calm bay. It is a meadow under the water, thick enough to vanish into.

oyster-bed.description: A rebuilt reef of small native shells. These are the Pacific coast's own kind, not the ones brought in from far away.

foxglove.description: Foxglove, brought in from away and poisonous in every part. It spreads too well in some places, so keep it for looks only.

mushroom-ring.description: A ring of woodland mushrooms in the leaf litter.

birch-tree.description: A slim birch with white bark, grown from a watered bed.

marsh-marigold.description: Gold marsh marigolds ringing the wet shallows in spring. They bloom before almost anything else, which shows the wet edge is working.

prickly-pear.description: Pad cactus with sweet fruit and bright blooms.

desert-marigold.description: Tough marigolds that glow against the sand.

moss-cushion.description: A springy cushion of moss campion and mountain avens. It is tight as a pillow and warm and damp inside.

sea-thrift.description: Pink sea-thrift pompoms. They love salt spray.

beach-shrub.description: Grey-green coastal scrub that puts up with salt. The wind cuts it flat on top and it stays thick underneath.

nectar-feeder.description: A sugar water feeder on a hook. It is fun to watch, but sugar water is not real food, so this is only a decoration.

crystal-cairn.description: A cracked geode set on stacked stones. A shiny desert landmark.

sun-totem.description: A carved sandstone totem topped with a desert crystal.

palo-verde-tree.description: The desert tree with green bark. Rare shade and yellow flowers for the scrubland.

shore-pine.description: A pine bent low and wide by salt wind. It holds the back dunes and blocks the wind off the water.

water-tupelo.description: A round-topped wetland tree with a swollen base standing in water. It comes from the far southeast, so here it is only for looks.

mesquite-tree.description: A low, spreading desert tree. Light shade and seed pods for the scrubland.

subalpine-fir.description: A slim, pointed fir that shrugs off deep mountain snow.

monterey-cypress.description: A coastal cypress pressed flat by the sea wind. It is planted here, not wild, since only two wild groves are left.

coast-live-oak.description: A wide evergreen oak. It holds the back shore and casts deep shade.

campfire.description: A crackling campfire ringed with stones. The heart of camp.

string-lights.description: A string of warm little lanterns to hang over your camp.

pinwheel.description: A bright pinwheel that spins in the breeze.

birdhouse.description: A little wooden house on a post. It looks charming even when nothing is home.

garden-gnome.description: A cheerful little gnome to watch over the garden.

wind-chimes.description: Driftwood chimes that sing softly when the wind moves through.

sundial.description: A carved stone sundial for telling time the slow way.

stone-cairn.description: A neat stack of smooth stones marking a quiet spot.

picnic-blanket.description: A checked blanket spread out for a sunny picnic.

insect-hotel.description: A frame packed with hollow stems, drilled blocks, and old bark, all under a small roof. The tubes come in every width, from pencil-thin down to a hair.

dry-stone-wall.description: A low wall of stacked stones laid with no cement. The gaps between them stay cool and shady.

bat-box.description: A tall, narrow wooden box with a rough inside and a slot along the bottom. Hang it high in the sun, and note the gap inside is barely wider than a finger.

leaf-litter-pile.description: A mound of damp leaves and moss left where it fell. It is warm in the middle and slowly turning into soil.

duck-nest-box.description: A wooden box on a pole standing over water. It has a round hole high on one side and wood shavings inside.

basking-log.description: A half-sunk log tilting up out of the water into full sun. The top stays dry and the bottom stays slick, and warming up out here really matters.

talus-pile.description: A jumble of broken rock with deep spaces between the blocks. Runs and hollows lead right down into the pile.

alpine-nest-shelf.description: A rock ledge lined with moss, out of the wind. A solid roof of rock hangs over it.

driftwood-pile.description: A tangle of sun-bleached driftwood, silver-grey and hollow-sounding. Damp shade hides under the lowest pieces.

nesting-bluff.description: A built-up sandy bank with narrow ledges cut into it. It drops away sheer below, out of reach from the ground.

pika-haypile.description: A stack of grass and flowers cut green and dried under a rock roof. It is packed tight and out of the rain.

snowbank-roost.description: A packed drift of late snow, firm on top and soft underneath. Inside a drift like this the wind stops completely.

whitebark-cache.description: A hidden store of pine nuts buried a few centimetres down. The seed is rich and oily and keeps all winter.

quartz-lantern.description: A stone lantern set with a glowing piece of quartz. It holds the last of the daylight.

home-rug.description: A soft woven rug to warm your floor.

home-table.description: A small wooden table with a sprig of flowers.

home-bookshelf.description: A shelf of field guides and well-read nature books.

home-fireplace.description: A crackling stone hearth that warms the whole room.

home-potplant.description: A leafy plant in a pot. A little bit of the meadow indoors.

home-painting.description: A framed painting of the preserve at its best.

home-sleeping-bag.description: A simple sleeping bag. Just the thing for a cozy night in the tent.

home-cushions.description: A pile of soft floor cushions to flop on.

home-stool.description: A simple stool with a cushion on top.

home-mushroomshelf.description: A little shelf dotted with woodland mushrooms.

home-reedmat.description: A woven reed mat from the marsh.

home-cactuspot.description: A tough little cactus in a clay pot.

home-driftwoodshelf.description: A shelf of worn driftwood holding beach finds.

home-wallclock.description: A handsome wall clock. A house needs one.

home-peltrug.description: A thick, warm rug for cold mountain nights.

home-chandelier.description: A grand candle chandelier. Just right for a lodge.

home-aquarium.description: A glass tank of clear water with a few little fish in it.

home-telescope.description: A brass telescope for the clear mountain sky.

dew-lantern.description: A glass globe of glowing morning dew that gives off a soft green light. It is made up, and just for looks.

stormglass-lantern.description: A shard of glass fused by lightning. It flickers with a cold light inside.

dragonfly-pond.description: A clear pool ringed with reeds. Open sunny water in the middle, with stems running from the bottom up past the top.

trail-tent.description: A snug canvas tent, a little home away from home. Step in and make it your own, and pitch one in each wild area past the meadow.

headlamp.description: A hand-wound lamp on a woven strap. Once made it is yours for good, and after dark it lights the ground around you.

binoculars.description: Hand-ground lenses in a woven grip. Once made they are yours for good, and what you have not written up yet gives a soft glint.

fellfield-gravel.description: Bare gravel that freezes and shifts every spring, held loosely by thin crusts of lichen. It looks like nothing, but only here will a cushion plant grow.

alpine-turf-mat.description: A tight mat of sedge, avens, and cushion plants over dark mountain soil. Turf like this takes years to close over bare ground and one summer of boots to open it up.

snowmelt-litter-mat.description: A soaked mat of last year's stems and leaves, let go as the snow pulls back. Almost all the rotting up here happens in these few damp weeks.

rotting-conifer-log.description: A well-rotted fir log lying where the drifts pile deepest. It is soft enough to push a finger into, and dead wood like this is a home, not a mess.

escape-cliff.description: A near-straight-up band of broken cliff, cut with ledges and footholds all the way. Nothing can be cornered on ground like this.

willow-basin-thicket.description: Low willow filling a sheltered dip, thick and buried by drifts each winter. Its buds and twigs stay in reach when everything else up here is under snow.

boulder-burrow-den.description: A deep burrow with many rooms, dug under a boulder well below the frost. Down there the cold hardly moves all winter.

inherited-earth-den.description: A hollow under boulders and roots, first dug by someone else, then made wider and taken over. Second-hand, and none the worse for it.

stonecrop-patch.description: Stonecrop wedged into gravel and rock cracks. Its fat leaves store water where there is almost no soil, and nothing else up high does the same job.

bumblebee-nest-burrow.description: An old tunnel in the turf, packed with dry grass and bedding. It is a ready-made room, warm and dark, that nobody had to dig.

chipmunk-burrow-larder.description: A shallow tunnel under a slab, with a side room packed full of seed heads. It stays dry and in reach all winter, though nothing in the game needs it now.

whitebark-pine.description: A whitebark pine grown from a seed that was buried and never dug up. Its cones do not open on their own, so it cannot spread without help.

old-woodpecker-cavity.description: A round hole cut into a dead trunk seasons ago and left empty since. The rim is still clean and the room below is dry.

snowfield-debris-line.description: A dark line of seed, pollen, and grit blown against the edge of a melting snowfield. It is a free delivery, carried uphill and dropped.

toad-upland-burrow.description: A borrowed tunnel in damp ground above a breeding pool. It sits below the frost and above the water, a place to wait out eight months.

treeline-log-den.description: A hollow log at the edge of the last trees, buried by drifts all winter. Tunnels run away from it under the snow.

fur-lined-prey-den.description: A den taken from whoever dug it, then lined with fur. Small, close and warm, with no work at all to do.

cliff-eyrie.description: A big stick nest on a bare cliff ledge. More sticks get added every year, and the same nest is used for decades.

ledge-natal-den.description: A dry overhang deep in broken cliff, hidden behind fallen rock. You cannot see it from below, and one narrow ledge is the only way in.

krummholz-bed-hollow.description: A shady scrape pressed flat into the ground under the bent pines. Out of the sun, out of the wind, and out of sight from above.

kelp-holdfast-reef.description: Clean rock on the shallow sea floor for kelp to grip. Kelp does not root in sand, so with no hard bottom the forest washes away.

nutrient-upwelling-current.description: Cold, rich water rising from the deep along the shore. It feeds this whole coast, and everything here runs on it.

coralline-algae-crust.description: Pink branching algae on low rock, like a rough turf. Surfgrass seeds have bristly arms that hook onto it, so no turf means no surfgrass.

low-tide-rock-bench.description: A wide shelf of bedrock that shows only at the lowest tides. It is the richest strip of shore, and it spends most of its time under water.

urchin-crevice-pit.description: Round hollows ground into solid rock, each a smooth bowl about a hand wide. Once a pit like this starts, it only gets deeper.

kelp-forest.description: Living giant kelp rising from the sea floor to a golden roof at the top. The water is dim green all the way up, and the fronds are thick enough to lie back in.

surfgrass-bed.description: A green meadow of surfgrass streaming in the surge on low rock. It grows so thick you cannot see the stone under it.

nearshore-spawning-shallows.description: Quiet water just off the surf line, thick with drifting food. It is warm on top and so calm that nothing sinks fast.

bare-sand-beach.description: Wide, flat, empty sand above the tide line. Bare sand matters on its own, so keep the view long and the surface untouched.

empty-shell-drift.description: A pocket of empty shells caught in a rock hollow, sorted by size by the waves. A beach with no spare shells is missing something.

subtidal-rubble-flat.description: Loose cobbles and broken rock just below the tide. Dead bits drift in and settle down between the stones.

surge-swept-rock-face.description: Open rock taking the full weight of the swell. It is hard to hold onto, and the water never stops moving past.

barnacle-crust-rock.description: A hard white crust welded across the upper rock. It is sharp underfoot, rough as coarse sandpaper, and stuck on like part of the stone.

protected-sand-gravel-flat.description: Firm sand and gravel behind a headland. It is easy to dig into, and calm enough that it stays right where it is.

benthic-amphipod-bed.description: Soft, deep mud along the kelp edge, packed with tiny tubes. There is so much life in it that the sea floor is more life than mud.

sheltered-cobble-field.description: Loose stones on a shore the surf never hits hard. Each one is damp and dark underneath, and the underside is the important part.

splash-zone-crevice.description: Dry-looking cracks in rock that the waves only reach as spray. It is the highest, driest step of the shore.

shell-dropping-rock.description: A flat, hard-topped boulder standing clear of the sand. Cracked shells lie on it, since a hard drop breaks them open.

swash-zone-runnel.description: The wet strip where each wave runs out and drains back. Every surge turns over the top few centimetres of sand.

plover-scrape-closure.description: A roped-off stretch of bare, open sand with light fencing and signs. There is nothing to build here, and what keeps it safe is that nobody walks on it.

high-tide-roost-rock.description: A raised rock that stays dry even at high tide. Open water rings it, so you can wait there when the flats are gone.

dune-manzanita.description: A low dune shrub that flowers in midwinter. It holds its berries deep into the cold months, when there is nothing else to eat behind the beach.

mussel-bed.description: A thick band of blue-black shells stacked two and three deep on mid-zone rock. They are packed so tight they hold each other up, and the gaps run right down to the stone.

sunlit-surge-pool.description: A deep pool washed by every wave and open to the sky. Food pours in from the rocks above, and full sun reaches the bottom.

offshore-nesting-island.description: A rock stack standing off the coast, with deep water all around. There is no way to walk onto it.

sandbar-loafing-roost.description: A low sandbar that dries out between tides. It is flat, open, ringed with water, and far enough out to be left alone.

haul-out-rocks.description: Low rocks and a sand spit with a wide quiet buffer around them. They slope up gently from the water, and crossing that buffer empties the place.

sheltered-rafting-cove.description: Calm water behind a point, inside the kelp. It stays flat as a pond even in a swell, with fronds lying loose on top.

creosote-bush.description: The main shrub of the desert flats, spaced far apart because its roots take all the water nearby. Its sticky leaves smell like rain and lose almost none of it.

saguaro.description: A giant column that stores months of rain in its pleated stem, swelling and shrinking with the season. Flowers on top, fruit in June, and a trunk soft enough to cut into.

cholla.description: A jointed cactus covered in barbed spines that come away at a touch. Inside the tangle of arms is a space almost nothing can push through.

desert-mistletoe.description: A leafless plant that roots inside mesquite and ironwood branches. It hangs in thick green-brown clumps and fruits in midwinter, when nothing else does.

chuparosa.description: A soft grey shrub with tube-shaped red flowers. It blooms right through the desert winter, when almost nothing else is out.

catclaw-acacia.description: A low thorny tree of desert washes, hooked all over with curved spines that catch as you pass. Thick cover above, and heavy seed pods by late summer.

bush-muhly.description: A fine-stemmed wild grass that grows up through shrubs for cover. It is the first thing grazed away, so seeing it back means the flat is healing.

cryptobiotic-crust.description: A living skin of tiny plants and lichen that knits bare soil together. It holds water and blocks weeds, and one boot print undoes years of it.

bare-ground-patch.description: A patch of soft, loose soil left open between the shrubs. It is loose enough to dig straight down into, but only where nothing has packed it hard.

harvester-ant-mound.description: A low mound capped with gravel, with a bare cleared ring around it and old seed husks at the rim. Whatever is under there moves a huge amount of soil.

buried-deadwood.description: Dead stems worked half down into the soil. Buried wood touches damp earth and breaks down, while wood on top just bleaches.

shrub-litter-mound.description: Leaves, stems, and husks blown into a heap under a shrub. It is dry and crackly on top, damp and dark underneath after rain.

termite-worked-litter.description: Soil laced with fine old tunnels and capped with litter stuck together. It is worked from below, and the tunnels let rain soak in instead of running off.

tortoise-burrow.description: A long, cool den with straight sides dug back into a bank, kept open by use. It goes far deeper than anything else out here and stays the same warmth all year.

caliche-shelter-cave.description: A hollow worn into a hard bank on a rocky slope. It is a ready-made room with a solid roof and no digging needed.

creosote-mound.description: Blown soil heaped around the base of a creosote and riddled with fine tunnels. The earth is loose and easy to work, and the shrub hides the doorways.

seed-larder-burrow.description: A shallow burrow under a shrub with side rooms packed with seeds. The doors get plugged with sand each dawn, which traps damp air inside.

deep-sand-burrow.description: A shaft that spirals two and a half metres down into loose soil. Down there the heat and dry air from above never reach.

kit-fox-den.description: A cool den with several doors, widened out of an older tunnel. The extra doors are ways to escape.

wash-bank-den.description: An earth den dug into the cut bank of a dry wash, above the flood line. It stays shaded, drained, and dry even when the wash runs.

snake-hibernaculum-desert.description: A deep rock crack that runs below the frost and stays above freezing all winter. The same crack gets used year after year, sometimes for decades.

saguaro-boot.description: The hard, waterproof scar a cactus grows around a hole in its trunk. It is a smooth flask of dried skin, and it lasts longer than the soft flesh around it.

thornscrub-stick-nest.description: A bulky stick platform wedged a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub. It is off the ground and too prickly for anything to follow.

carrion-patch.description: Something that has died, left where it fell instead of hauled away. In a few days almost nothing is left, and all of it is back in the soil.

saguaro-fruit-fall.description: Split red cactus fruit at the height of the June heat, just before the rains. For a few weeks it is the richest food and the wettest drink in the desert.

pollinated-cactus-fruit.description: Prickly pear and cholla hanging heavy with ripe fruit. A crop this big only sets when every flower was dusted first, and out here that is never sure.

shade-form-scrape.description: A shallow scrape dug in the deep shade under a shrub, down to cool soil. It is ten degrees cooler than the open ground a metre away.

browse-exclosure.description: A low fence around a patch of young oaks. Nibbled hard, they never pass knee height, but inside the fence acorns become trees.

nurse-log-seedbed.description: A rotting, mossy log lying on the forest floor. Seeds that land on bare leaves die, but those on rotten wood grow into trees.

deep-duff-soil.description: Years of old leaf mould, never raked and never driven over, threaded with roots and fungus. This is where the forest fungus really lives.

truffle-patch.description: Fungus lumps that grow underground on oak and hemlock roots. Nothing shows on top, so the crop has to be sniffed out.

soft-rot-snag.description: A small dead stub whose wood has gone soft and pale. You can press a thumbnail into it, and that is what makes it easy to work.

rotting-heartwood-log.description: A log rotted hollow down the middle while its outer shell still holds. Inside it is dark, damp, and shut off from the weather.

downy-cavity.description: A round hole about as wide as a thumb, cut into a dead trunk one season and left. It is small, dry, and already made.

pileated-cavity-snag.description: A big dead trunk with a deep square hole cut last spring, wide enough for an arm. A fresh one gets cut each year, and the old ones stay.

flooded-cavity-snag.description: A dead trunk standing in shallow water with an old hole high up. Below the hole there is nothing but open air, then several metres down, water.

bark-slab-snag.description: A dying tree whose bark has curled away from the trunk in loose slabs. Behind each slab is a warm, dry gap barely wider than a finger.

leaf-drey.description: A ball of leaves and twigs the size of a football, wedged into a high fork. It is woven from the inside out and rebuilt every year.

larder-burrow.description: A burrow door no wider than a coin, with tunnels running metres underground. They lead to a nest room and a store holding more than a litre of seeds.

hemlock-stand.description: A close-grown clump of hemlocks that hold the snow off the ground. Their shade keeps the stream cold, and the inner bark stays in reach all winter.

browse-thicket.description: Thick young regrowth in a gap where a big tree came down. Every twig is in reach from the ground.

crayfish-shallows.description: A stony, ankle-deep edge of loose flat rocks over gravel. Dark gaps back up underneath every one of them.

root-mass-den.description: The dry hollow left under the tipped-up roots of a fallen tree. Earth and roots make the roof, and it is sheltered from every side but one.

earth-den-bank.description: A well-drained slope with a den dug back into it and several doors along the face. It gets made bigger and reused for years rather than dug fresh.

snake-hibernaculum-forest.description: A deep crack filled with rubble, running below the frost line. It stays cold but never freezes, right through to spring.

broken-top-chimney.description: A big living tree snapped off high, rotted hollow inside. The open chimney is a foot across, and only a very old tree rots this way.

hollow-denning-tree.description: A living tree with a rotted-out room high in the trunk. It is dry inside and metres above the ground, out of reach from below.

rocky-den-ledge.description: A dry gap under a leaning slab of rock, screened by brush and open at both ends. Sheltered, but easy to slip out of at the first sound.

adopted-stick-nest.description: A bulky old pile of sticks and leaves left in a high fork. It is worn and a bit saggy but still sound, and ready to use in midwinter.

bare-soil-scrape.description: A patch raked back by hand to bare, open soil. Bare ground counts too, since seedlings need somewhere that is not covered.

native-thistle-stand.description: A wild prairie thistle, not one of the weedy kinds from Europe. It has deep tube-shaped flowers and seed heads that break open into soft down.

grass-thatch-litter.description: A deep mat of dead grass stems, leaves, and roots left where they fell. Meadow fungus pulls it apart and hands it back to the soil.

grasshopper-egg-pod-bank.description: A strip of firm, sun-warmed bare soil at the edge of the grass. It is packed hard enough to hold a drilled hole open all winter.

vole-runway-network.description: Narrow runways clipped through thick grass at ground level. They link burrow doors and grass-lined rooms, like little highways hidden under the thatch.

milkweed-rhizome-bed.description: A spreading bed of showy milkweed grown from root cuttings. The stems bleed white sap when they break, and one bed slowly becomes a patch.

bumblebee-nest-tussock.description: A thick clump of unmown grass sitting over an old hole in the turf. It is warm, fur-lined, dry, and completely hidden from above.

brush-form-hollow.description: A shallow scrape pressed into the grass under low brush. It is a resting spot, not a burrow, so no digging is needed.

serviceberry-browse-thicket.description: A wild shrub with soft twigs and fat buds that stay above the snow. By late summer it hangs heavy with purple fruit.

milkweed-aphid-colony.description: Bright orange specks packed tight along milkweed stems, thick enough to hide the green. Do not spray them, since every milkweed patch gets them and does fine.

squirrel-burrow-town.description: A burrow system with many doors dug into deep open soil, its mounds spread across a wide patch. Long after it is left, the tunnels stay open.

mantis-ootheca-stem.description: Stiff dead stems left standing through winter, with a hard tan foam case glued to one. Cut the stems back in autumn and you cut out what is inside.

domed-grass-nest-tunnel.description: A grass-roofed nest cup woven down into deep bunchgrass, with a covered run leading in. Only a real spread of wild grass is thick enough to hide one.

bluebird-nest-box.description: A wooden box facing open grass, with a small round hole and a metal guard on the pole below. The hole is cut to one exact width, and that width is the whole design.

snake-hibernaculum-meadow.description: A room of rock and soil dug below the frost line, often started from an old tunnel in the bank. There is space down there for a great many at once.

deep-loam-soil-bank.description: A bank of deep, soft, stone-free soil with nothing hard to hit. Soil like this can be dug faster than it can be walked over.

earthen-fox-den.description: A south-facing bank widened into a den with several exits, made from an older burrow. It is dry, warm early in the year, and quick to leave.

crown-stick-eyrie.description: A big stick platform wedged into the top of the tallest tree. It looks out over open grass, and more sticks go on each year.

sunlit-mudflat.description: A bare shelf of wet, sun-warmed mud at the water's edge. Cattail seed is tiny and needs light, so it will not sprout in shade.

clearwater-shallows.description: Slow water with the silt settled out, so light reaches the bottom. Plants under the water live on that light, so clear water comes first.

detritus-drift.description: A sunken raft of dead cattail and sedge leaves going soft under fungus. More energy moves through a marsh as dead plants than as live ones.

crayfish-burrow-bank.description: A soaked clay bank riddled with finger-wide tunnels. Each one holds water even when the marsh drops low in late summer.

submerged-spawning-slab.description: A flat stone just under the surface with a clear gap below. The underside is smooth, shady and clean.

stable-silt-shoal.description: A wide shelf of silt and fine sand where the water moves slowly. It is soft enough to sink into and firm enough not to shift.

cattail-root-shallows.description: Shallow water over a thick mat of cattail roots, packed down into the mud. They are starchy and swollen, and in reach from below even when the top is frozen.

flooded-reed-clump.description: A tight stand of cattail and reed stems in ankle-deep water. They are stiff enough to hold a weight slung between them, and the water underneath is what makes it safe.

winter-litter-mound.description: A deep pile of damp leaves, loose bark, and old stems heaped on dry ground by the marsh. It is deep enough that the middle never gets as cold as the air.

vernal-pool.description: A shallow, separate pool that fills with snowmelt and dries right up by late summer. The drying is the point, since nothing that needs water all year can settle in.

wet-meadow-margin.description: A band of damp, grassy meadow between the marsh and dry land. It is never flooded and never fully dry, and the marsh needs it.

sandy-nest-bank.description: A warm, drained rise of sand and fine gravel above the waterline. It is loose enough to dig and quick to drain, and banks like this are rarer than they look.

crane-nest-mound.description: A wide heap of marsh plants piled up in open shallow water. Its top stands well clear of the water, so anything coming close has to wade.

hidden-reed-platform.description: A low platform of living reeds bent down and woven together deep in a thick stand. It sits barely a hand above the water and cannot be seen from any side.

cut-bank-burrow.description: A bare, upright earth bank rising straight out of the water. It is soft enough to tunnel a metre back into and firm enough that the tunnel holds.

overwater-thicket.description: Low willow and alder leaning out over deep still water. Their branches hang a metre above the surface, with cool shade underneath.

muskrat-bank-den.description: An old bank burrow with its door below the waterline and its room dry above. Someone else dug it, and it has stood empty since.

otter-bank-den.description: A roomy bank den with an underwater door and a dry room above. It is almost always taken over from an older burrow rather than dug fresh.

beaver-pond.description: Deep, lasting water held back by a dam of sticks and mud, with drowned trees still standing in it. It is deeper and more open than cattail marsh, and it will not appear on its own.

beaver-canal.description: A shallow dug channel running from the pond out into the marsh. It is just deep enough to float a branch, and it keeps open water joined up through a dry summer.

rotting-log-crumble.description: A soft, damp, half-rotted log going back to soil. It falls apart when you lift it, and the air under it stays wet all day.

orb-web-anchor-stems.description: Tall dry stems left standing in a sunny gap. They are stiff enough to hold a line of silk pulled tight between them.

bat-maternity-roost.description: A narrow, dark crack high off the ground, with full sun on the rock outside. It stays warm all day and is tight enough to press against on both sides.

barn-loft-nest-box.description: A deep wooden box mounted high under a gable, open on one side. There is a lip of straw across the sill, and it is dark and dry inside.

coyote-natal-den-bank.description: A den dug into a brushy bank, usually an old hole made wider. It gets used hard for a few weeks and then left.

damp-leaf-corner.description: A shady corner where fallen leaves pile up and go soft. It stays damp under there even in a dry week.

goat-cliff-ledge.description: A narrow shelf cut across a near-straight cliff face, scraped bare and dusty. It is no wider than a doormat, on ground far steeper than most would try.

alpine-mineral-lick.description: A damp bank of salty earth, gnawed and licked into a hollow. Spring grass has no salt in it, and there is nowhere else this high to get it.

deep-snow-den.description: A tunnel driven metres down into a drift that lasts into late spring, winding past buried boulders. Side rooms hold frozen food, and it only works where the snow stays.

deep-canyon-edge.description: The place where the sea floor stops and drops away into cold blue-black deep. Deep water, right up against the coast.

breaking-surf-line.description: A clean line of waves standing up and toppling along an open beach. It is a moving wall of white water the whole length of the shore.

eelgrass-grazing-lawn.description: A patch of eelgrass cropped short and kept that way. The blades stay young and tender instead of growing long and tough.

saguaro-crown-nest.description: A bulky stick platform wedged where a tall cactus splits into arms. It is wide enough for a whole family, with a wall of spines below that nothing can climb.

tarantula-silk-burrow.description: A thumb-wide hole in firm ground, its rim smoothed and bound with silk. A few trip-lines fan out over the sand, and whatever made it may keep it for twenty years.

elk-wallow.description: A churned muddy dip in a forest opening, kept wet and bare by something heavy rolling in it. The puddle left behind holds water for weeks.

bramble-ground-nest.description: A grass-lined cup set level with the leaf litter under a bramble arch. Nothing above it but thorns, and that is the whole defence.

eagle-nest-crown.description: The top of the tallest living tree on the marsh, holding a stick nest the size of a bathtub. The same nest gets added to year after year until the branch finally gives way.

still-water-cove.description: A pocket of open water behind the reeds where the wind never reaches. The surface is smooth as glass, with a few stems drifting on it.

winter-sleep-burrow.description: A tunnel under a tilted slab leading to a grass-lined room below the frost line. No store and no side rooms, just somewhere to lie still until spring.

moth-scree-crack.description: A dark slot under a loose slab of scree, cool, still, and dry. It runs back further than the daylight reaches, so the heat never gets to the end.

swift-cliff-seam.description: A narrow upright crack running up a sheer rock face, far too tight to stand in. The only way in is head-first, and the only way out is a drop.

wild-grape-tangle.description: A woody vine roped up a leaning trunk, heavy with fruit by late summer. It is a ladder and a larder at once.

snake-egg-mound.description: A heap of rotting wood chips and bark piled against a cut stump. As it rots it runs warm, and that warms what is buried in it.

willow-thicket-swale.description: A damp hollow behind the dunes, filled with low willow and bramble. It is tangled right down to the ground, so nothing big can push in.

canyon-ledge-den.description: A dry overhang cut back into a canyon wall, screened by fallen slabs. It is shaded all day, hidden from below, and reached by one route only.

puffball-turf-ring.description: A ring of pale domes pushing up through old turf. Step on a ripe one and it smokes.

sedge-tussock-nest.description: A thick, knee-high clump of sedge in a damp low spot. It is packed so tight you could push a fist deep inside and never find the hole again.

hidden-grass-nest.description: A thick tuft of grass left standing in a damp hollow. The middle is pressed down into a deep cup you would walk right past.

cocoon-leaf-drift.description: A drift of curled fallen leaves banked against a log. Silk cases are wrapped in leaves that fell with them, so the whole lot lies here all winter.

acorn-cache-scatter.description: A patch of soft open ground pocked with little digs. Acorns went in one at a time, and the ones left grow into oak seedlings.

winter-freeze-litter-bed.description: A shallow bed of loose leaves over soft soil, only a few inches deep. That is deep enough, since it freezes and thaws with the ground.

canopy-nest-limb.description: A heavy flat limb against the trunk of an old tree, high where the leaves close over. It is thick enough to hold a big nest for years, with clear flying room below.

thicket-bed-hollow.description: A scooped, dusty hollow under thick thorn bushes, lain in all through the heat of the day. The shade counts more than the cover.

falcon-scrape-ledge.description: A gravel shelf high on a cliff with a shallow dip kicked in it. Nothing is built here, and nothing needs to be.

octopus-den-midden.description: A dark crack under a boulder with a rock pulled part-way across the door. Outside is a tidy heap of empty, drilled shells, and that heap is how you find it.

meadow-mushroom-ring.description: A curved arc of pale button caps pushing up through damp grass after rain. The ring is the edge of a fungus growing outward under the ground.

bracket-fungus-shelf.description: Overlapping fans of banded fungus stepping up the side of a dead log. This is the thing eating the wood, and the log only turns to soil because of it.

wild-celery-bed.description: Long ribbon leaves streaming underwater in the shallows, rooted in silt. It lives only on the light that reaches the bottom, so the water must be left to settle clear.

snowbank-mushroom-cluster.description: A crowd of small pale mushrooms with hairy stems, growing on buried rotten wood. They come up right at the edge of a melting drift, while snow is still on the ground.

grizzly-dig-slope.description: A high bank of loose earth threaded with roots, soft enough to tear open. The turned soil is left lying in heaps.

feather-lined-crack.description: A narrow dry crack in a wind-scoured rock face. The back of it is packed with down and fur.

borrowed-burrow-mouth.description: A burrow mouth someone else dug, widened and swept clean. A fan of loose sand spreads out at the door.

browsed-pond-shallows.description: A soft-bottomed edge where the water is chest-deep and thick with stems. It has been cropped short in ragged patches.

waterfall-splash-ledge.description: A wet shelf tucked behind a thread of falling meltwater. It is mossy and always in shadow.

grub-digging-ground.description: A patch of soft leaf-mould soil left loose, already pitted with small cone-shaped holes. Something has been turning it over.

clifftop-burrow.description: A round hole driven back into deep turf right at the top of a sea cliff. The earth is worn bare at the door.

groundhog-burrow-mound.description: A fan of fresh-turned earth banked around a round hole. A second hole hides in the grass a few paces off.

opossum-den-hollow.description: A dry hollow under a leaning log, open at both ends. The floor is covered with dragged-in leaves.

shore-stick-nest.description: A bulky platform of salt-bleached sticks wedged in a high fork. It gets added to and patched every season.

happy-buddha.description: A round little figure sitting cross-legged, both arms thrown up and grinning. Rubbing the belly is meant to be lucky, and the clay has gone smooth and shiny there.

lucky-toad.description: A fat little three-legged toad sitting on a pile of coins.

rippled-sand-bed.description: Clean sand below the low tide line, combed into even ridges. The current is gentle enough to leave them standing.

rock-crevice.description: Stacked slabs with narrow shady cracks. They run back further than you can see.

heron-rookery.description: A stand of tall dead trees holding a dozen big stick platforms.

basket.description: For gently picking up light things that grow back: seeds, berries, flowers, fiber, shells.

2.effect: Hold up to 350 things. Pick up 2 light ones at a time.

shovel.description: For carefully digging stones, clay, and sand, and getting ground ready.

2.effect: Shape mud banks and burrow mounds. Dig up 2 things at a time.
Carry 2 water at a time. Dry ground heals faster.
