kind.amphibian: Frogs and salamanders are back in {biome}. That is a sure sign the water and damp ground are healthy.

narrative.allkinds: Every kind of animal now lives in {biome}. From the smallest bug to the top hunter. A whole community.

combo.meadow-fox-prey: Foxes and their prey are both back in Willow Meadow. Foxes keep mice and rabbits from getting too many. That stops the grass from being eaten down, so the meadow stays richer.
combo.forest-bobcat-prey: A bobcat hunts Old Hollow Forest again. It sneaks up close, so it needs thick cover. That is just what you built.
combo.forest-cavity-reuse: A woodpecker cut a hole, used it once, and left. Another animal moved right in. In a forest, one bird’s old home is another’s new one.
combo.wetland-beaver: The beaver is back. It builds the place everyone else needs. Its dams raise the water and make new ponds. Fish, frogs, and birds all use them.
combo.wetland-beaver-wake: Otters and herons followed the beaver in. They hunt in the deep, still water its dams make. That water would not be here without it.
combo.wetland-heron-hunt: A great blue heron works the shallows. It stands still for minutes. Then it strikes faster than you can see.
combo.desert-snake-rodent: The rattlesnake is back, and it earns its keep. It waits and finds prey by body heat with pits on its face. It keeps desert mice in check.
combo.desert-coyote-prey: A mountain-lion roams the scrubland again. It hunts mice and rabbits. That keeps the whole desert food web in balance.
combo.desert-shared-burrow: Nobody wastes a hole in the desert. The tortoise digs a burrow, and a burrowing owl takes the spare room. A few feet down it stays cool while the top bakes.
combo.alpine-eagle-prey: A golden eagle watches the ridge. It can see a yellow-bellied-marmot from over a mile away. Then it dives faster than a car on the highway. It is the top hunter up here.
combo.coastal-keystone: The ochre sea star is back. It was the first animal ever called a keystone. Take it away and mussels cover every rock. Bring it back and the whole tidepool shares the space.
combo.coastal-otter-kelp: An otter floating offshore means a forest below. Otters eat the urchins that would chew the kelp down to bare rock.

total.total-25: Twenty-five kinds of animal live here now. The quiet you found is well and truly gone.

health.25: {biome} is a quarter healed. Bare ground is turning into real habitat. The first tough animals can risk it now.
health.80: {biome} is doing well at 80%. It can now feed its top hunters and a whole food web.

meadow.damaged: Bare, dusty ground where a flowering meadow used to be. The native grasses went, so the bugs went. Then everything that ate them went too.
meadow.restored: A whole grassland food web, top to bottom. Healthy meadows like this hold carbon in their deep roots. They also feed a third of the bugs here.
meadow.coexistence: The fox and the hawks only move in once the mice and rabbits are back. Hunters come last, when there is enough to eat.

forest.damaged: A logged woodland. The big trees and dead standing trees are gone. So woodpeckers have nowhere to carve. And the animals that reuse their holes never come.
forest.thriving: Three layers of forest now: floor, middle, and top. Each one has its own animals. Flying squirrels glide between the trees you grew.
forest.coexistence: A big woodpecker cuts a hole, uses it once, and leaves it. Then a wood duck, a flying squirrel, or an owl moves in.

wetland.recovering: Water is back in the channels and the reeds are growing. Frogs, dragonflies, and water striders come first. Herons follow the frogs into the shallows.
wetland.restored: A whole wetland, from crane to minnow. It cleans all the water that flows out of it. That quiet work keeps the whole river healthy.
wetland.coexistence: The beaver builds what everyone else needs. Its dam makes the deep, still water where otters hunt and herons wait.

desert.damaged: A flat with no brush and no burrows, eaten bare. With no way to escape the heat, even the toughest animals stay away.
desert.restored: The hardest land here, fully alive. An elf owl in the cactus and a desert-tarantula under a stone. You cannot flood a desert back. You have to shade it back.
desert.coexistence: In the desert nobody wastes a hole. A tortoise digs a burrow, and a burrowing owl takes the spare room under the brush.

alpine.damaged: A worn alpine slope. The wildflower turf is rubbed down to bare rock. Up here healing takes tens of years, not seasons.
alpine.recovering: Turf is growing back over the rock. Pikas carry hay into the rocks. Marmots sun on the boulders. Rosy-finches work the melting snow.
alpine.coexistence: When the eagle circles the ridge, the marmots whistle and the whole slope goes still. That alarm ties the high country together.

coastal.damaged: A worn shore with washed-out dunes and empty tidepools. Without dune grass to hold the sand and kelp to feed on, the tide has nothing to give.
coastal.recovering: The dunes are holding and the tidepools are filling with crabs, anemones, and mussels. Gulls and plovers work the tide line again.
coastal.restored: The wildest stretch here, whole again. From whale spouts to clams. Two key animals do the quiet work that keeps it in balance.
coastal.coexistence: Two animals run this shore. The sea star keeps mussels off every rock. The otter eats the urchins that would mow down the kelp.

meadow: Wind moves through the grass in long silver waves. Somewhere a sparrow answers it.
The meadow smells of warm earth and crushed clover after you turn the soil.
Grasshoppers spring out of the grass ahead of your steps like little sparks.
Seed heads nod on their stalks, scattering next year's meadow on the breeze.
Dew beads the spiderwebs strung between the grass blades at first light.
A puff of wind sends dandelion seeds past you. They drift by like tiny parachutes.
The light goes gold and low across the grass tips toward evening.
Crickets tune up in the warm grass — a sound you feel as much as hear.
Morning fog catches in the grass and burns off in ribbons as the sun climbs.
A meadow is never really quiet. Even at night the crickets keep talking.
Wild grass sends roots three times deeper than the grass is tall. That is where a meadow keeps its strength.
Most of what a meadow stores is under the ground. That is why a good meadow can take a fire or a dry year.
Wild flowers and bees grew up together. A flower's shape often fits the tongue of the bee it likes best.
Birds that nest on the ground need tall grass to hide in. A neat lawn is empty to them.
Voles cut little paths through the thick grass. Almost every meadow hunter feeds along those paths.
Meadow flowers bloom one after the other all season. So there is always something to feed the bees.
Clover pulls plant food out of the air and into the soil. It feeds the whole meadow for free.
Crab spiders hide inside flowers. They match the petals so well that bees never see them coming.
Goldfinches wait to nest until the thistles go to seed. That way the chicks come when the food does.
One square foot of good meadow soil can hold more living things than there are people on Earth.
A grasshopper can jump 20 times its own length. That is like you jumping over a bus.
One ladybug can eat 5,000 aphids in its life. That is why gardeners love them.
Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed. They store its poison. That makes them taste awful.
A bumblebee's buzz is not its wings. It is shaking its own muscles to knock pollen loose.
A killdeer will act like its wing is broken to lead a hunter away. Then it gets up and flies off.
Butterflies taste with their feet before they decide to feed.
Crickets chirp faster when it is warm. Count the chirps and you can guess how warm it is.
A meadowlark is not a lark at all. It is a cousin of the blackbird, with a song like a flute.
One dandelion can send off 2,000 seeds. Each one gets its own tiny parachute.
A bluebird in the grass can see a caterpillar fifty feet away.
Swallows drink while flying. They skim low and sip from a puddle without landing.
Garter snakes cannot hurt you. But they are bad news for the slugs and mice you do not want around.
Bees carry pollen for the flowers. The flowers feed the young bees. Neither would last long alone.
Where a fox hunts, the rabbits keep moving. The grass they leave alone grows back thick.
The hawk above and the snake in the grass hunt the same voles from two sides.
Monarchs go where milkweed grows. Milkweed spreads wherever the meadow is left wild.
Rabbits nibble the grass low in patches. Birds that feed on the ground love the open lanes they leave.
Sparrows and finches eat the seeds the meadow drops. Then they drop what they do not use. They are gardeners with wings.
The first big wave of wild flowers has opened. Color is coming back to the meadow.
The bare patches are knitting closed — green is winning back the dust.
Butterflies are everywhere now. The meadow has hit its stride.
The meadow hums now in a way it did not when you got here. That low buzz is the sound of a healthy place.
Swallows work the bugs above the grass at dusk; hard to believe this was bare dirt.
That whir at dusk is a nighthawk. It flies with its mouth open, scooping bugs out of the air.
A praying mantis is like a tiny tiger. It grabs bugs much bigger than itself.
Leafcutter bees cut neat circles out of leaves. They use them to line their nests, one at a time.
A bare patch of ground in the sun turns into a runway. Ground bees and lizards come there to warm up.
Foxes have whiskers on their legs as well as their faces, feeling their way through the tall grass.
The deeper the roots go, the more rain a meadow drinks before any runs off.
Painted lady butterflies fly farther than almost any other. They cross whole lands.
By late summer the meadow is mostly seed. It is a feast for every bird that comes by.
Fox on the ground and hawk in the air — the meadow's voles are hunted from both worlds now.
Butterflies, bees, and beetles are all working the same flowers. The whole pollen crew is here.
An owl has taken the night shift over the meadow. It hunts the mice the day birds never see.
Deer and rabbits eat the same grass at different heights. Between them they keep it from taking over.
A berry bush next to a shrub gives food and a place to hide. That is just what small birds want.
A wild flower patch and a bee garden are both in. This corner is a bee highway now.
A brush pile and a rock pile are both down. Now everything from voles to snakes has cover.
Oak and willow are both rooted now. At last the meadow has real shade to give.
A pond to drink from and a bath to splash in — the meadow's birds have both now.
forest: Light falls in green shafts through the canopy, shifting as the leaves move.
The forest floor is springy under your feet. It is made of hundreds of years of fallen leaves.
Somewhere above you a woodpecker drums on a hollow trunk. It sounds like a knock at a door.
The air here is cool and damp and smells of moss and old wood.
A branch creaks. A squirrel scolds. Then the forest goes quiet again.
Early in the morning mist hangs low between the trunks. It is slow to lift under the trees.
Mushrooms came up overnight along a fallen log. They look pale against the dark wood.
Leaves spiral down one at a time, each a slow green-gold parachute.
A wren sings from the low brush. The song is far bigger than the bird that made it.
Rain doesn't fall so much as drip here, handed down leaf by leaf from the canopy.
Dead trees left standing are called snags. They hold more life than almost anything in the forest. Animals carve homes in them and use them again and again.
An old forest grows in layers. There is the floor, the low brush, and the treetops. Each layer holds different life.
Under the soil, fungus ties tree roots together. The trees trade water and food through it.
A rotting log is not waste. It is a pantry that feeds bugs, fungus, newts, and the soil for years.
Big trees pull water up from deep down and breathe it into the air. They make their own weather.
Forest soil holds a huge amount of carbon. Dig it up and most of that goes into the sky.
Many forest seeds need an animal to bury or carry them. The forest plants itself.
Owls fly almost without a sound. The edges of their feathers are like combs, and they break up the noise of the air.
Bats can eat their own body weight in insects in a single night.
Salamanders breathe partly through their skin. They need a damp, shady forest floor to live.
Flying squirrels do not really fly. They glide on a flap of skin between their legs and steer with the tail.
A pileated woodpecker hunts ants in wood. It can chop a hole big enough to fit your fist.
Banana slugs can be bright yellow and as long as your hand. They clean the forest floor as they crawl.
Black bears climb trees to nap on the branches. They wedge in and look quite comfy.
A chickadee calls dee-dee-dee. The more dangerous the hunter it sees, the more dees it adds.
Newts can be so poisonous that a hunter is sorry it ever tried.
Squirrels will sometimes pretend to bury a nut. It fools any thief that is watching.
A bear can smell thousands of times better than we can. It can pick up food from miles away.
Wood ducks nest in tree holes. On their first day the ducklings jump from the hole to the ground.
Some forest fungus glows softly in the dark. People once called it foxfire and used it to mark trails.
A woodpecker carves a hole, uses it once, and leaves. Then the rest of the forest moves right in.
The owl hunts the night shift, the hawk the day — between them, few mice go uncounted.
Squirrels bury more nuts than they ever dig up. The ones they forget grow into the next forest.
A bobcat needs thick cover to sneak up close. That is just the brush you brought back.
Bats and owls split the night. One takes the bugs, the other takes the mice. By morning the forest is a quieter place to be small.
Young trees are taking hold in the open ground. The low layer of the forest is finding its feet.
The treetops are closing over your head. The ground below is cooling into real forest.
Three layers of forest now: the floor, the brush, and the treetops. Each has its own life.
The woods feel old again, the kind of quiet that takes decades to grow back.
Moss holds rain like a sponge. It lets the water out slowly, so the forest floor never fully dries.
One oak can feed and shelter over 2,000 kinds of life. It is a whole world in one tree.
Porcupines have around 30,000 quills, each tipped with tiny barbs.
Nuthatches walk down tree trunks head first. They spot bugs the climbers going up miss.
Dead wood left to rot gives more back to the forest than living wood ever does.
The fisher is quick enough to flip a porcupine over. Very few hunters can eat one safely.
Tree rings hold a record of dry years, fires, and good years. It is a diary written in wood.
The low bushes feed the deer and the berries feed the birds. Nothing here goes to waste.
A woodpecker's tongue is very long. When it is not in use it wraps around the back of the skull.
Ravens copy sounds and work out puzzles. They also seem to roll and tumble in the air just for fun.
Fallen leaves keep bugs safe all winter. Those bugs are the first food of spring.
Spotted towhees dig loudly in the leaves. You would swear it was something much bigger.
A forest cools the air around it. Step under the trees on a hot day and you will feel it.
Two kinds of owl now split the night between them. The forest dark is well hunted.
The big woodpecker carves the holes and the wood ducks take them. It is housing, forest style.
A big hunter walks these woods again. The whole forest is more awake because of it.
Squirrels by day, flying squirrels by night. The treetops and the tree holes are busy all the time.
A dead tree still standing and a nesting tree, side by side. The woodpeckers carve, and everyone else moves in.
A mushroom log and a hollow log are both rotting down. The fungus is fed, the newts have shelter, and the soil is built back.
A woodland pool beside a fern spring. That gives the salamanders the damp they must have.
A berry bush in the brush with ferns below it. That is food and cover on the forest floor at once.
wetland: Reeds rattle softly in the wind. Somewhere out there a frog clears its throat.
The water lies still and dark, doubling the sky and the reeds along its edge.
A dragonfly darts back and forth above the water. Its wings catch the light.
Mud sucks at your boots near the bank, rich and black and full of life.
Rings spread on the water where something came up to feed, then went back down.
The marsh smells green and mineral, of wet earth and growing reeds.
Blackbirds sway on the cattails. They flash their red shoulders and call out.
Mist sits on the water at dawn until the first heron steps through it.
A water strider skates on top of the water. It dents the surface but never breaks it.
The frogs go quiet as you walk by. Then they start again behind you, one brave voice at a time.
Wetlands clean dirty water and hold back floods. They do for free what costs cities millions.
Frogs and newts breathe partly through their skin. So when they are here, the water is clean.
A marsh grows more life than almost any place on Earth. It can match a rain forest.
Reed beds are nurseries. Countless young fish, frogs, and bugs hide among the stems.
Wetlands refill the water under the ground. They let rain soak in slowly instead of rushing off.
Cattails clean the water as they grow. They pull the extra plant food up into their stalks.
Many birds fly thousands of miles from one wetland to the next. Lose one and the whole trip breaks.
The mud at the bottom of a marsh can hold carbon for thousands of years.
A frog changes jobs as it grows. Egg, tadpole, and adult each fill a different spot in the food web.
Still water grows warm and rich; moving water stays cool and clear. A marsh needs both.
Dragonflies have hunted these skies for over 300 million years. They are older than the dinosaurs.
A dragonfly catches its prey in the air more than 9 times out of 10. Few hunters do better.
A beaver's front teeth never stop growing. Chewing wood is what wears them down.
Some turtles can breathe through their back end. That helps a lot in a winter spent under water.
A heron's neck has a special hinge that lets it strike like a loosed spring.
An otter keeps a favorite rock as a tool. It tucks it into a pocket of loose skin.
Bitterns point their bills skyward and sway with the reeds to vanish in plain sight.
On a calm night you can hear a bullfrog from half a mile away.
A kingfisher hangs in the air, then dives head first. It shuts a third eyelid like a pair of goggles.
Muskrats build little lodges and eating huts out of the reeds they cut.
The beaver doesn't move into habitat — it builds it. Its dam makes the deep water everyone else needs.
Otters and herons both hunt the still water the beaver's dam holds back.
The heron hunts the shallows where the frogs hide. The frogs eat the bugs the reeds shelter.
Turtles sun themselves on the logs that otters and muskrats leave floating. Nothing is wasted here.
Where there are tiny fish there are kingfishers. The marsh feeds upward from the smallest fish.
The water is finding the old channels again. The reeds are coming up to meet it.
The marsh is loud now — frogs, blackbirds, the whir of dragonflies all at once.
Open water, reed bed, and mud bank are all here at once. The marsh looks like a marsh again.
Standing at the water's edge, it's hard to picture the cracked mud you started from.
Sandhill cranes pair for life. They dance to win each other: bowing, leaping, tossing grass in the air.
The edge of a wetland is where water meets land. It holds more life than either side alone.
A leopard frog can jump many times its own length. At the first scare it is gone into the water.
Mergansers have saw-edged bills. That is how they hold the slippery fish they chase under water.
People once stuffed life jackets with cattail fluff. The marsh has always been useful.
A damselfly folds its wings along its back when it rests. A dragonfly holds its wings out flat.
A beaver pond slows the water so the mud can settle. Everything downstream runs clearer.
Marsh wrens build several fake nests. A hunter has to guess which one holds the eggs.
A green heron will drop a feather or a bug on the water as bait. Then it grabs the fish that comes.
Whirligig beetles have split eyes. They watch above and below the water at the same time.
One acre of healthy marsh can hold thousands of birds in a season. Some nest, some just pass through.
Cattail roots were a staple food here long before there were towns to drain the marsh.
Beaver and otter are both working the water. The marsh has its builder and its swimmer.
A heron in the shallows and fish in the water below it. The marsh food chain is joined up.
A tall marsh bird stalks the reeds again, patient as the water itself.
Turtles share the basking logs by day; nothing here wastes a sunny perch.
A reed bed and a cattail stand together. That is a nursery and a hiding place for half the marsh.
A lily pool above a mud bank — frogs get sun and ooze both, just how they like it.
A nest platform over the water and logs to sun on. The marsh birds and the turtles are both set.
Bulrush and sedge tussocks give the marsh wrens a whole maze to hide their nests in.
desert: Heat shimmers off the flats, and the only sound is the wind moving sand grain by grain.
A roadrunner darts between the brush, all legs and purpose, and is gone.
The light is huge here, and the shadows under each shrub are sharp and cool.
At dusk the desert lets out its breath. The heat lifts and the night shift starts to move.
A lizard does push-ups on a warm stone, claiming the rock for itself.
The brush smells of dust and resin, sharpened by the heat.
Once the sun is down, the stars come out thick and close over the desert.
Tracks cross the sand from the night before — a story of who went where in the cool dark.
A cactus wren rattles from a cholla, scolding no one at all.
After a rare rain the whole flat turns a little green. Everything races to bloom before it dries.
Many desert animals never drink at all. They get their water from the seeds they eat and from their own bodies.
A burrow is the desert's cool room. A few feet down it stays mild while the top bakes.
A cactus opens its tiny holes at night, not in the day heat. That way it loses as little water as it can.
Desert soil has a living crust of moss and lichen that holds it together. One footstep can undo years of it.
Seeds can wait years in the desert soil for the one good rain that makes blooming worth it.
Shade is worth a lot here. One nurse plant can shelter a dozen young plants under it.
Desert hunters work at dawn and dusk. That way they miss both the heat and the deep cold of night.
A saguaro can take 50 years to grow its first arm and live for over 150.
Pack rats build big trash piles. The dry air keeps them, so they hold thousands of years of desert history.
The desert lives in bursts. Long waits, then a wild rush of life after rain.
A kangaroo rat never drinks. It can live its whole life without one drop.
A horned lizard can shoot blood from its eyes to scare off a hunter.
A roadrunner can run more than 20 miles an hour. It would rather run than fly.
An elf owl is smaller than a soda can. It nests in holes woodpeckers leave in the cactus.
A desert-tarantula can go months without a meal. It can live for many years.
Gila woodpeckers drill nest holes in the big cactus. Later, many other animals use them.
A jackrabbit lets heat out through its huge ears. Hold one up to the sun and you can see the blood inside.
Some desert toads sleep under the ground most of the year. They come up only for the rains.
A chuckwalla squeezes into a rock crack. Then it puffs up so tight that nothing can pull it out.
A kit fox's big ears let heat out. They also pick up the tiniest rustle of a beetle in the dark.
No hole goes to waste in the desert. The tortoise digs it and the owl takes the spare room.
A rattlesnake finds its prey by body heat. It keeps the mice in check, and it waits as long as it takes.
A mountain-lion eats whatever the desert has. That is what keeps the whole web from tipping over.
The woodpecker carves the cactus. Elf owls and flycatchers move into the holes it leaves.
Quail move in flocks. Dozens of eyes watch for the hawk so each bird can keep eating.
Brush is taking hold, and with it the first scraps of shade the flat has had in years.
Burrows dot the ground now. The desert's life has a place to get out of the sun.
Cactus, brush, and burrow are all in place. The scrubland is working the way a desert should.
At dusk the whole flat comes alive with rustles and calls; the dead heat is long gone.
In spring the Costa's hummingbird dives to show off. The sun flares purple off its throat.
An agave can grow for many years, bloom once in a tall spike, and then die. It does it all on one water budget.
Antelope squirrels run with their tails flipped over their backs. They look like little sun shades.
A desert night can be 40 degrees cooler than the same spot at noon.
The phainopepla eats mistletoe berries. Wherever it lands, it plants the next crop.
Banded geckos squeak when grabbed and can drop their tail to make a clean escape.
Desert bees nest in the ground and time their whole lives to a few weeks of bloom.
Dry channels carry the rare flood. The biggest brush always grows along their banks.
A creosote bush can copy itself for thousands of years, all from one first plant.
Scorpions glow an odd blue-green under a black light. No one is quite sure why.
Most lizards would die at the body heat a desert iguana works in.
A hard, sudden rain can fill a dry channel in minutes. That is a flash flood.
A tortoise burrow with an owl living in it. Desert housing is fully booked.
A rattlesnake and a kangaroo rat share the same flat. Hunter and hunted, and the desert holds its balance.
A desert hunter walks the flats after dark now, reading the sand for tracks.
The woodpecker drills the cactus and the elf owl takes the hole. The big cactus is a block of flats.
A burrow mound and a shaded rock shelter give the desert two ways to duck the sun.
Cactus and brush together give shade, cover, and food. There used to be nothing here but bare ground.
Marigolds and a nectar feeder are out. Now the hummingbirds have a reason to come this way.
Mesquite and palo verde are the desert's nurse trees. They shade every young plant that starts under them.
alpine: The wind never quite stops up here; it leans on the grass and combs the snowfields.
Far below, the lower country lies hazed and small; up here the air is thin and bright.
A yellow-bellied-marmot whistles. The sound bounces off the rock and the whole slope seems to listen.
Cloud shadows slide across the rock. For a moment the mountain goes dim, then it blazes again.
Melted snow runs between the stones. It is ice cold and so clear you can see every pebble.
Cushion plants hug the ground in tight green mounds, out of the wind's reach.
The quiet up here feels heavy. Only the wind and a falling stone break it.
Wild flowers crowd a sheltered dip. They bloom hard and fast in the short mountain summer.
Frost still rims the shadows at midday where the sun hasn't reached.
A pika runs across the rocks with a mouthful of flowers. It is racing the coming winter.
Mountain plants grow low and slow against the cold. Some are hundreds of years old and only inches wide.
Snow works like a blanket. Many small animals spend the winter in the mild gap between snow and ground.
Mountain soil is thin and very old. One inch of it can take a thousand years to build.
Up here summer is a sprint. Plants must sprout, bloom, and seed in just a few short weeks.
When the snow melts sets the clock for the whole mountain. Everything blooms and breeds to match it.
Lichen grows on bare rock less than a millimetre a year. It is the slow first settler of the heights.
Cold, clean meltwater holds more air in it. That is why mountain trout can live there.
The short, bent trees up at treeline can be very old. Hundreds of years of wind twisted them into shape.
Mountain plants and animals are a warning sign. As it warms they can only climb, until there is no mountain left.
A mountain meadow may bloom all at once. It is racing the snow that comes back in a few weeks.
Pikas do not sleep through winter. They spend all summer stacking hay to eat under the snow.
A golden eagle can spot prey from over a mile away. It dives at more than 150 miles an hour.
Mountain goats are not really goats. They climb near-straight cliffs on soft, gripping hooves.
In winter the white-tailed-ptarmigan turns white to hide. It also grows feathered snowshoes on its feet.
A Clark's nutcracker can hide tens of thousands of pine seeds. It remembers where most of them are.
A yellow-bellied-marmot can sleep for eight months of the year. Its heart barely ticks over.
Bighorn rams crash heads at 20 mph; their skulls are built with a double layer to take it.
In winter the ermine turns from brown to pure white. Only the tip of its tail stays black.
Rosy-finches nest higher than almost any other song bird. They nest right up in the snow.
The snowshoe hare changes color with the seasons. It is brown in summer and white in snow.
When the eagle circles, the marmots whistle and the whole slope goes still. That warning ties the heights together.
The nutcracker plants the pines it forgets. The whole treeline moves uphill on what one bird cannot recall.
Pikas and marmots share the rock pile. One stacks hay while the other suns on the boulders above.
The ermine follows the voles into the gap under the snow. It hunts where the cold cannot reach.
The trout hold in the snowmelt pools. The eagles and martens learn just where to watch.
Turf is closing back over the bare rock, a tiny bit at a time.
Wild flowers have taken the sheltered dips. Now the marmots have a spot worth sunning in.
Turf, a snowmelt pool, and rocky shelter are all in place. The high country is whole again.
An eagle could circle this ridge now and find a slope full of life beneath it.
Boreal toads climb higher than you would think. They breed in snowmelt ponds that dry up by late summer.
Mountain bluebirds hang in the air like little hawks, then drop on bugs in the grass.
Whitebark pines count on one bird. The nutcracker plants nearly all their seeds.
Mountain air holds less of what we breathe. So the animals up here have blood that makes the most of it.
Pine grosbeaks hardly mind people at all. Old-timers called them mope-heads.
A yellow-bellied-marmot town keeps lookouts. One whistle and the whole slope is empty in a heartbeat.
Snow hangs on in the shade of boulders into midsummer. It waters the flowers downhill of it.
Up here a warm rock in the morning sun is the best spot on the whole mountain.
Glacier lilies push up right at the edge of the melting snow. They bloom before anything else.
The song of a white-crowned sparrow shifts from one mountain to the next. Each range has its own tune.
Alpine chipmunks spread their seeds among dozens of hidden stores. That is how they last the winter.
The treeline is not really a line. It is the forest slowly giving in to wind and cold.
A pika stacks hay while a yellow-bellied-marmot suns above it. The rock pile is full up now.
An eagle circles and the marmots below whistle the warning. The whole slope works as one.
A cliff-climber has claimed the crags, picking its way where nothing else dares.
A small, fierce hunter works the rock pile now. It slips between the stones after voles.
A snowmelt pool beside mountain flowers. Water and food both, in the short mountain summer.
A mat of heather and a cushion of moss. Together they hold the thin soil against the wind.
Bent pine and mountain fir hold the treeline. They are the last trees before the bare heights.
A burrow mound tucked into a rock pile. The pikas and marmots have their fort.
coastal: The surf comes in long and steady, and the whole shore breathes with it.
Gulls circle and squabble along the tide line. They pick through what the sea left behind.
The air is all salt and kelp and cold spray off the breakers.
A wave pulls back and the tidepools fill up. Each one is a tiny world of color.
Sandpipers chase the water out, then run from the next wave. Over and over, never quite caught.
Fog rolls in off the water and turns the whole coast soft and gray.
Sea glass and shell fragments glint where the last high tide stranded them.
The rocks are slick with weed and loud with the suck and hiss of the surge.
A brown-pelican glides a hand's width above the swell. It rides the cushion of air the wave makes.
Out past the breaking waves the sea lifts and falls, slow and huge and uncaring.
Tidepool animals live two lives. They take crashing waves and then hours out in the air.
Kelp can grow two feet in a day. It builds forests under water that shelter hundreds of kinds of life.
Dune grasses anchor the shore with deep roots — without them, one storm can wash a beach away.
The line of stranded kelp feeds a whole crowd of bugs, birds, and crabs.
Mussels and barnacles strain the sea water. They clear it as they feed.
Life in a tidepool sorts into bands. It depends on how long each one can stand being out of water.
River mouths and shorelines are nurseries. The fish born there later fill the open sea.
Anemones sting their prey with harpoon cells too small to feel through your skin.
Acre for acre, eelgrass beds store carbon faster than a rain forest.
Shore birds on the move plan their stops around the tides. They feed on what the water uncovers.
Sea otters hold hands while they sleep. That way the water does not pull them apart.
A sea star can push its stomach out of its body. That way it can eat prey too big to swallow.
Hermit crabs move to bigger shells as they grow. Sometimes they line up and swap in size order.
A group of pelicans is called a squadron. They dive for fish from as high as 60 feet.
An octopus can taste with its arms. It can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak.
A sea star can grow a lost arm back. A few can grow a whole new body from one arm.
Sanderlings run on legs that blur like clockwork as they chase the waves.
A barnacle glues its own head to the rock. Then it kicks food into its mouth with its legs.
Harbor seals can sleep under water. They come up to breathe without ever waking.
Gray whales make one of the longest trips of any animal with fur. It is thousands of miles each way.
The sea star was the first animal we called a keystone. Take it away and mussels take every rock. Put it back and everything shares the space.
An otter offshore means a forest below it. It eats the urchins that would mow the kelp down to stubs.
Pelicans and cormorants follow the fish that the kelp shelters. The forest below feeds the birds above.
Oystercatchers pry open the mussels the tide has fed. They work one rock at a time.
Where anemones and mussels share a rock in peace, thank the sea star that walks it.
The dunes are holding and the tidepools are filling. The shore is finding its feet.
Crabs, anemones, gulls — the wrack line and the rocks are busy again.
A held dune, a full tidepool, kelp along the tide line. The whole shore is working as one.
From a whale's spout to a clam's straw, the coast hums with life. It runs from deep water to dry sand.
A green sea turtle can hold its breath for hours while it rests on the bottom.
A mussel holds on with tiny threads. For their size they are stronger than steel cable.
A dolphin sleeps one half of its brain at a time. That way it never stops coming up to breathe.
Snowy plovers nest in a bare dip in the open sand. That is why a quiet beach matters so much.
Kelp grips the rock with a holdfast, not roots. It drinks straight from the sea water.
Turnstones flip stones and seaweed to find the small life hiding under them. That is how they got the name.
Bat stars come in a riot of colors, no two quite the same.
The highest tides come with the new moon and the full moon. They reach places the sea rarely touches.
The Anna's hummingbird dives from high up. Its tail feathers make a sharp note as it falls, all to win a mate.
Pigeon guillemots flash bright red feet and mouths as they court along the cliffs.
A falling tide opens a whole world. In a few hours it will be under water again.
Beach hoppers bury themselves in wet sand by day. After dark they swarm the tide line.
A sea star walks the rock and anemones hold their spot below it. The tidepool shares fairly now.
Otter and seal both offshore — the kelp beds are rich enough to feed them both.
Pelicans and cormorants dive the same shoals. The fish that the kelp shelters feed the wings above.
Shore birds are working the open sand again. They race the waves for what the water uncovers.
A tidepool and a line of kelp together. The crabs and gulls have both a home and a feast.
Dune grass and beach shrub anchoring the sand — the shore can hold a storm now.
Eelgrass and oyster beds are straining the shallows. The water clears and the fish come back.
There is safe nesting ground above the tide line. At last the shore birds can raise young here.
